LAB 8: Model-based Requirements Documentation Department of Software Engineering  2026 Department of Software Engineering  2026 
Objective  
To illustrate the process of requirements documentation using use case diagrams and use case specifications, highlighting their roles in capturing system functionality, interactions, and user goals, with practical examples to demonstrate their application in software development. 
Theoretical Description 
Requirement models are used in addition to natural language requirements documentation and partly replace requirements that would have been documented using natural language.  
Model:  
A model is an abstract representation of an existing reality or a reality to be created. In order to construct conceptual models, specific modeling languages are used. A modeling language is defined by its syntax and semantics: 
Syntax: The syntax of a modeling language defines the modeling elements to be used and specifies the valid combinations thereof.  
Semantics: The semantics defines the meaning of the individual modeling elements and serves therefore as a foundation for the interpretation of the models of the respective modeling language. 
UML  
The unified modeling language (UML) is a general-purpose visual modeling language that is intended to provide a standard way to visualize the design of a system. 
Use Cases 
Use cases were first proposed as a method to document the functionalities of a planned or existing system on the basis of simple models. The use case approach is based on two concepts that are used in conjunction with one another, i.e. Use case diagrams and Use case specifications.  
 
 
 
Use Case Diagrams  
Use case diagrams in the UML are simple models to schematically document the functions of a system from a user’s perspective and to document the interrelations of the functions of a system and the relations between these functions and their environment.  Department of Software Engineering  2026 Department of Software Engineering  2026 
Modeling Elements of UML Use case Diagrams 
 
Figure 3: Essential Modeling elements of Use Case Diagram 
Use Case 
In the use case modeling approach, functional requirements are described in terms of actors, which are users of the system, and use cases. A use case defines a sequence of interactions between one or more actors and the system. In the requirements phase, the use case model considers the system as a black box and describes the interactions between the actor(s) and the system in a narrative form consisting of user inputs and system responses.   
A use case always starts with input from an actor. A use case typically consists of a sequence of interactions between the actor and the system. Each interaction consists of an input from the actor followed by a response from the system. Thus, an actor provides inputs to the system and the system provides responses to the actor. The system is always considered a black box, so that its internals are not revealed. Whereas a simple use case might involve only one interaction between an actor and the system, a more typical use case will consist of several interactions between the actor and the system. More complex use cases might also involve more than one actor. Department of Software Engineering  2026 Department of Software Engineering  2026 
Consider a simple banking example in which an automated teller machine (ATM) allows customers to withdraw cash from their bank accounts. There is one actor, the ATM Customer, and one use case, Withdraw Funds, as shown in Figure 4. The Withdraw Funds use case describes the sequence of interactions between the customer and the system; the use case starts when the customer inserts an ATM card into the card reader, then responds to the system’s prompt for the PIN, and eventually receives the cash dispensed by the ATM machine. 
 
Figure 4: Example of Actor and Use Case 
Names begin with a verb – A use case models an action so the name should begin with a verb. 
Uses cases that are defined for the system are depicted using oval shapes. These shapes contain the name of the use case. 
Identifying Use cases 
To determine the use cases in the system, it is useful to start by considering the actors and the interactions they have with the system. Each use case describes a sequence of interactions between the actor and the system. In this way, the functional requirements of the system are described in terms of the use cases, which constitute a functional specification of a system. However, when developing use cases, it is important to avoid a functional decomposition in which several small use cases describe small individual functions of the system rather than describe a sequence of events that provides a useful result to the actor. 
 
Let us consider the banking example again. In addition to withdrawing cash from the ATM, the ATM Customer actor is also allowed to query an account or transfer funds between two accounts. Because these are distinct functions initiated by the customer with different useful results, the query and transfer functions should be modeled as separate use cases, rather than being part of the original use case. Thus, the customer can initiate three use cases, as shown in Figure 5: Withdraw Funds, Query Account, and Transfer Funds. Department of Software Engineering  2026 Department of Software Engineering  2026 
 
Figure 5: Banking System Actor and Use Cases Actors:  
Actors are outside the system boundary and represent people or systems that interact with the system modeled.  An actor represents a role played in the application domain, typically by a human user. A user is an individual, whereas an actor represents the role played by all users of the same type. For example, there are several customers in the Banking System, who are all represented by the ATM Customer actor. Thus, ATM Customer actor models a user type, and individual customers are instances of the actor. 
An actor is very often a human user. For this reason, in UML, an actor is depicted using a stick figure. In many information systems, humans are the only actors. In other systems, however, there are other types of actors in addition to or in place of human actors. Thus, it is possible for an actor to be an external system that interfaces to the system. In some applications, an actor can also be an external I/O device or a timer. External I/O device and timer actors are particularly prevalent in real-time embedded systems, in which the system interacts with the external environment through sensors and actuators. Department of Software Engineering  2026 Department of Software Engineering  2026 
Actors are depicted by a stick figure that receives the name of the actor and is tagged with the stereotype “actor”. If the actor is a system, a rectangle may be used in conjunction with the stereotype “system”. 
Primary and Secondary Actors  
A primary actor initiates a use case. Thus, the use case starts with an input from the primary actor to which the system has to respond. Other actors, referred to as secondary actors, can participate in the use case. A primary actor in one use case can be a secondary actor in another use case. At least one actor must gain value from the use case; usually, this is the primary actor. An example of primary and secondary actors is shown in Figure 6. The Remote System actor initiates the Generate Monitoring Data use case, in which the remote system sends monitoring data that is displayed to monitoring operators. In this use case, the Remote System is the primary actor that initiates the use case, and the Monitoring Operator is a secondary actor who receives the monitoring data and, hence, gains value from the use case. 
 
Figure 6: Example of primary and Secondary Actors 
System boundaries:  
System boundaries within a use case diagram separate the parts of the use case that are part of the system from the parts (people or systems) that are outside the system boundary.  Optionally, the name of the system may be denoted at the system boundary in the diagram. 
Use Case Relationships 
Include relation:  
 
An include relation from one use case to another use case depicts that the interaction sequence of the first use case includes the interaction sequence of the other use case. Few things to consider when using the <include> relationship.  Department of Software Engineering  2026 Department of Software Engineering  2026 
The base use case is incomplete without the included use case.  
The included use case is mandatory and not optional. 
Include relationship between use cases is shown by a dashed arrow with an open arrowhead from the including (base) use case to the included (common part) use case. The arrow is labeled with the keyword «include». 
 
Figure 7: Example of an Inclusion Use Case and Include relationships 
Figure 8: Example of Inclusion Use Case Department of Software Engineering  2026   Department of Software Engineering  2026   
 
Extend relation:  
Extend relationships represent exceptional or seldom invoked cases. The exceptional event flows are factored out of the main event flow for clarity. Use cases representing exceptional flows can extend more than one use case. 
The direction of an <extend> relationship is to the extended use case. 
It extends the base use case and adds more functionality to the system.  
The use case that is extended is referred to as the base use case, and the use case that does the extending is referred to as the extension use case. It is important to note that the base use case does not depend on the extension use case. The extension use case, on the other hand, depends on the base use case and executes only if the condition in the base use case that causes it to execute is true. 
Extend relationship is shown as a dashed line with an open arrowhead directed from the extending use case to the extended (base) use case. The arrow is labeled with the keyword «extend». 
 
Figure 9: Example of Extend relationship 
 
An extend relation depicts that an interaction sequence that belongs to use case A extends some interaction sequence in use case B at a specified point. This is known as the extension point. Department of Software Engineering  2026 Department of Software Engineering  2026 
The extension is triggered by the condition defined. 
 
Figure 10: An example using modeling elements of use case diagram 
Generalization  
In this case, the specializing use cases or actors inherit the properties of the generalizing use case or actor. For instance, the actors “service mechanic” and “customer service representative” can be generalized as the actor “employee”. The generalizing actor would carry all aspects that the actors “service mechanic” and “customer service representative” have in common (e.g., employee ID) 
For example, in the banking example there might be a use case called “Pay Bills”. This can be generalized to “Pay by Credit Card”, “Pay by Bank Balance” etc. 
 
Figure 11: Example of Generalization Use Case 
 
Use Case Specifications 
Use cases diagrams do not document any information about the individual use cases such as the systematic interaction between a use case and an actor. Department of Software Engineering  2026 Department of Software Engineering  2026 
There are different templates for textual specification of use cases. These templates define types of information that should be documented for a use case and suggest an appropriate structure for the information. The template references therefore document experience-based knowledge regarding structured textual documentation of use cases.  
Main Scenario and Alternate Scenario 
The main sequence of the use case describes the most common sequence of interactions between the actor and the system. There may also be branches off the main sequence of the use case that describe less frequent interactions between the actor and the system. These alternative sequences are deviations from the main sequence that are executed only under certain circumstances– for example, if the actor makes an incorrect input to the system. The alternative sequences are also described in the use case. In the Withdraw Funds use case, the main sequence is the sequence of steps for successfully achieving a withdrawal. Alternative sequences are used to address various error cases, such as when the customer enters the wrong PIN and must be re prompted, when an ATM card is not recognized or has been reported stolen, and so on. Each sequence through the use case is called a scenario. A use case usually describes several scenarios, one main sequence and a number of alternative sequences. Note that a scenario is a complete sequence through the use case, so a scenario could start out executing the main sequence and then follow an alternative branch at the decision point. For example, one of the Withdraw Funds scenarios starts with the main sequence of the customer inserting the ATM card into the card reader, entering the PIN number in response to the prompt but then receiving an error message because the PIN was incorrect, and then entering the correct PIN. 
Preconditions and Postconditions 
Preconditions define prerequisites that must be met before the system can begin executing the use case. The system should be able to test all preconditions to see if it’s possible to proceed with the use case. Preconditions could describe the system state (for a use case to withdraw cash from an automated teller machine, the ATM must contain money), but they don’t describe the user’s intent (“I need some cash”). Checking preconditions can prevent some errors that might otherwise take place if the system knows at the outset that it can’t successfully complete the use case but proceeds anyway. If the ATM is empty, it shouldn’t let a user even begin a withdrawal transaction. This is a way to make your applications more robust. Users aren’t likely to be aware of all of a use case’s preconditions, so the BA might need to get some input from other sources.  Department of Software Engineering  2026 Department of Software Engineering  2026 
Postconditions describe the state of the system after the use case executed successfully. 
Postconditions can describe:  
Something observable to the user (the system displayed an account balance).  
Physical outcomes (the ATM has dispensed money and printed a receipt). 
Internal system state changes (the account has been debited by the amount of a cash withdrawal, plus any transaction fees)

LAB 10: Requirements Validation and Negotiation Department of Software Engineering  2026 Department of Software Engineering  2026 
Objective  
This lab manual is designed to provide hands-on experience with the concepts of Requirements Validation and Negotiation. The labs cover fundamental techniques, quality aspects, validation methods, and negotiation processes crucial for effective requirements engineering in software development. 
Theoretical Description 
Requirements Validation and Negotiation  
Validation and negotiation during requirements engineering is meant to ensure that the documented requirements meet the predetermined quality criteria, such as correctness and agreement. 
Quality Aspects of Requirements 
A major aim of using quality criteria (e.g., completeness, understandability, agreement) in requirements validation is to be able to check requirements systematically. In order to assure an objective and consistent validation, it is necessary that each quality criterion is concretized and refined. In correspondence with the overall goals of the requirements engineering process, the validation is carried out with the following goals:  
Content: Have all relevant requirements been elicited and documented with the appropriate level of detail?  
Documentation: Are all requirements documented with respect to the predetermined guidelines for documentation and specification?  
Agreement: Do all stakeholders concur with the documented requirements and have all known conflicts been resolved? 
Each of the three goals implies an individual approach that focuses on specific aspects of the quality of the requirements. Therefore, the following three quality aspects have been defined: 
Quality aspect “content”  
Quality aspect “documentation”  
 
Quality aspect “agreement”  
A requirement should be approved for further development activities only if all three quality aspects have been checked.  Department of Software Engineering  2026 Department of Software Engineering  2026 
Quality Aspect “Content” 
The quality aspect “content” refers to the validation of requirements with respect to errors in the content.  
Test criteria of the quality aspect “Content” 
The validation of requirements about the quality aspect “content” is successful once requirements validation has been applied to the following error types and no significant shortcomings have been detected:  
Completeness (set of all requirements): Have all relevant requirements for the system to be developed (for the next system release) been documented? 
Completeness (individual requirements): Does each requirement contain all necessary information?  
Erroneous Requirement: “The software should generate reports.” 
This requirement is incomplete as it does not specify the types of reports needed, the data to be included in the reports, the format or structure of the reports, or the intended audience for the reports. 
Revised Requirement: The software should generate monthly sales reports that include product sales, revenue, and customer demographics. The reports should be presented in PDF format and be accessible to managers for analysis and decision-making. 
Traceability: Have all relevant traceability relations been defined (e.g., to relevant requirements sources)? 
Erroneous Requirement: "The system shall provide real-time updates to users about their account status." 
 
Traceability Relation: This requirement is linked to the user interview notes where users expressed a need for real-time account updates (Interview Note 5), and to the stakeholder meeting where this feature was prioritized (Stakeholder Meeting Minutes, April 2024). Department of Software Engineering  2026 Department of Software Engineering  2026 
Correctness/adequacy: Do the requirements accurately reflect the wishes and needs of the stakeholders?  
Consistency: Is it possible to implement all defined requirements for the system to be developed jointly? Are there no contradictions? 
Erroneous Requirement-1: “The software should be accessible for visually impaired users, following WCAG 2.1 Level AA guidelines.” 
Erroneous Requirement 2: “The system should have color-coded elements to highlight important information.” 
The requirements conflict in terms of accessibility and design choices. While one requirement emphasizes accessibility for visually impaired users, following specific guidelines, the other requirement introduces a design element that relies on color-coding. This inconsistency needs to be addressed to ensure the software meets both accessibility and design requirements. 
No premature design decisions: Are there any forestalled design decisions present in the requirements not induced by constraints (e.g., constraints that specify a specific clientserver architecture to be used)?  
Erroneous Requirement: "The system shall use a MySQL database to store user information." 
This requirement specifies the use of MySQL, which is a design decision that should be determined during the design phase based on various factors like performance, scalability, and compatibility. 
Revised Requirement: "The system shall store user information in a database that meets performance and scalability requirements." 
Rationale: The revised requirement avoids specifying the type of database and instead focuses on the functional need, allowing for flexibility in the design phase. 
Verifiability: Is it possible to define acceptance and test criteria based on the requirements? Have the criteria been defined?  
 
Erroneous Requirement: "The software should be flexible. " Department of Software Engineering  2026 Department of Software Engineering  2026 
The requirement lacks specificity and measurable criteria to determine flexibility. Without clear definitions or specific functionalities related to flexibility, it becomes challenging to verify or assess the level of flexibility provided by the software. 
Necessity: Does every requirement contribute to the fulfillment of the goals defined? 
Erroneous Requirement: “The mobile banking application should have social media integration to allow customers to directly share their banking activities, such as transactions and account balances, on popular social media platforms.” 
While social media integration may seem like an appealing feature to some customers, it is not essential for the core functionality and security of a mobile banking application. It introduces potential security risks and raises privacy concerns. 
Feasibility 
Confirm the requirement can be implemented within technical, organizational, legal, and financial constraints.  
Erroneous Requirement: “The system should process one million transactions per second on a low-end server.” 
This requirement may not be feasible due to hardware limitations. Achieving such high transaction processing capacity on a low-end server may not be technically possible or economically viable. 
Unambiguous 
Ensure the requirement is understood in only one way by all readers. 
Erroneous Requirement: “The system should have fast performance.” 
The term "fast" is subjective and open to interpretation. It does not provide a clear benchmark or specific measurable criteria for performance.  
Revised Requirement: The system should load the homepage within 3 seconds for 90% of users. 
 
 
Quality Aspect “Documentation” 
The quality aspect “documentation” deals with checking requirements with respect to flaws in their documentation or violations of the documentation guidelines that are in effect, such as understandability of the documentation formats and the consideration of organizational or project specific guidelines regarding the documentation of requirements but also the structure of the requirements documents.  Department of Software Engineering  2026 Department of Software Engineering  2026 
Four test criteria of the quality aspect “documentation”  
Requirements validation with regard to the quality aspect “documentation” is successful when requirements validation has been applied to the following error types and no significant shortcomings have been detected:  
Conformity to documentation format and to documentation structures: Are the requirements documented in the predetermined documentation format? For instance, has a specific requirement template or a specific modeling language been used to document the requirements? Has the structure of the requirements document been maintained? For instance, have all requirements been documented at the position defined by the document structure?  
Erroneous Requirements:

Rationale: Enhance security by verifying user identity. 
Fit Criterion: The system must not allow login without a password.

Conformity to documentation rules: Have the predetermined documentation rules and documentation guidelines been met? For instance, has the syntax of the modeling language been used properly?

Quality Aspect “Agreement” 
The quality aspect “agreement” deals with checking requirements for flaws in the agreement of requirements between stakeholders. During the course of requirements engineering, stakeholders gain novel knowledge about the system to be developed. Due to this additional knowledge, the opinion of the stakeholders regarding a requirement that has already been agreed upon can change. During requirements validation, stakeholders have the opportunity to requests changes without impairing the subsequent development activities. Department of Software Engineering  2026 Department of Software Engineering  2026

Requirements Validation Techniques:  
Commenting: During commenting, the author gives their requirements to a co-worker for expert review, who identifies and marks quality issues like ambiguity or errors, briefly explaining the flaws. 
 
Inspections: Inspections of software or any other type of product are done to systematically check development artifacts for errors by applying a strict process. An inspection is typically separated into various phases: planning, overview, defect detection, defect collection, follow-up, and reflection.  Department of Software Engineering  2026 Department of Software Engineering  2026 
Walk-throughs: A walk-through is a lightweight version of an inspection. A walkthrough is less strict than an inspection and the involved roles are differentiated to a lesser degree. The goal of a walk-through of requirements is to identify quality flaws within requirements by means of a shared process and to gain a shared understanding of the requirements between all the people involved. 
Perspective-based reading: Perspective-based reading validates requirements by checking them from different viewpoints, such as the user, software architect, and tester, to ensure they meet desired functions, design needs, and test case derivation requirements. 
Validation through prototypes: Requirements validation with prototypes allows stakeholders to experience and test requirements, identifying errors and discrepancies. Prototypes can be throw-away, discarded after use, or evolutionary, developed further for future use.  
Using checklists for validation: Checklists for requirements validation consist of questions/statements that help detect errors, considering multiple aspects in complex environments. Sources for checklist creation include quality aspects, validation principles, document/individual requirements criteria, auditor experiences, and error statistics. LAB 11: Requirements Management Department of Software Engineering  2026 Department of Software Engineering  2026 
Objective  
The objective of the lab for requirements management is to train participants in effectively managing requirements throughout the project lifecycle, including assigning attributes, establishing traceability, versioning, condensing views, and prioritizing requirements. 
Theoretical Description 
Requirements management comprises purposefully assigning attributes to requirements, defining views on requirements, prioritizing requirements, and tracing requirements as well as versioning requirements, managing requirements changes, and measuring requirements. Requirements management includes the management of individual requirements as well as the management of requirements documents. 
Attribute Scheme  
The set of all defined attributes for a class of requirements (e.g., functional requirements, quality requirements) is called an attribute scheme. Attribute schemes are usually tailored to meet the individual project’s needs. The reader of the requirement (e.g., the contractor, product manager, developer, project manager) can find information of the same type in the same position (e.g., the requirement stability is always in the template section “stability”). It is harder for her to overlook important information and that this information, supported by the structure of the template and the predetermined attribute values, can be documented purposefully and correctly.

LAB 12: Requirements Prioritization Department of Software Engineering  2025 Department of Software Engineering  2025 
Objective  
The objective of the lab for requirements prioritization is to equip participants with the skills to systematically evaluate and rank requirements based on factors such as business value, urgency, feasibility, and stakeholder needs, ensuring clear and consistent prioritization throughout the project lifecycle. 
Theoretical Description 
Requirements prioritization is the systematic process of ranking requirements based on their importance, value, urgency, and feasibility. It ensures that critical requirements are addressed first, optimizing resource allocation and project outcomes. Prioritization involves evaluating requirements using various criteria, such as stakeholder needs, business value, technical complexity, and potential risks. Common techniques for requirements prioritization include 
MoSCoW (Must have, Should have, Could have, Won't have), Ranking, Top-Ten, and the 100Point Method. By effectively prioritizing requirements, teams can focus on high-impact features, minimize scope creep, and maintain alignment with project goals. 
Requirements Prioritization  
Requirements are prioritized during requirements engineering using different prioritization criteria in all sub-activities. Requirements can be prioritized by their order of implementation, for example. Due to the different prioritizations in the various sub-activities, the priority of a requirement can be determined by one or more attributes (e.g., priority of the contractor, priority due to urgency of implementation). 
In order to prioritize a set of requirements, a goal (i.e., purpose) of prioritization must be defined first. In addition, the constraints of prioritization are documented, such as the availability of different stakeholders and groups thereof or the resources available for prioritization. 
Depending on the goal of prioritization, the criterion for prioritizing the requirements (or the combination of two or more criteria) is chosen. The following are typical examples of prioritization criteria: 
Cost of implementation 
 
Risk  
Damage due to unsuccessful implementation  Department of Software Engineering  2025 Department of Software Engineering  2025 
Volatility  
Importance  
Duration of implementation (i.e., how long it takes to be implemented) 
Techniques for Requirements Prioritization  
For prioritization, multiple techniques exist. The techniques mainly differ with regard to the time and effort needed but also with regard to the suit ability of the different prioritization criteria and project properties. 
Ranking and Top-Ten Technique  
Ranking: In this technique, a number of selected stakeholders arrange the requirements to be prioritized with respect to a specific criterion.  
 
Top-Ten Technique: In this technique, the n most important requirements for a defined criterion are selected. For these requirements, a ranking order is determined afterward. This ranking order represents the importance of the selected requirements with regard to the defined criterion.  
Single-criterion Classification  
Another prioritization technique that is often used in practice is based on the classification of requirements with respect to the importance of the realization of the requirements for the system’s success. This type of prioritization is based on assigning each requirement to one of the following priority classes.  
Mandatory: A mandatory requirement is a requirement that must be implemented at all costs or else the success of the system is threatened.  
 
Optional: An optional requirement is a requirement that does not necessarily need to be implemented. Neglecting a few requirements of this class does not threaten the success of the system.  Department of Software Engineering  2025 Department of Software Engineering  2025 
Nice-to-have: Nice-to-have requirements are requirements that do not influence the system’s success if they are not implemented.  
Kano Classification  
Kano Model Can classify and prioritize requirements with respect to their acceptance in the market. 
Dissatisfiers: A requirement specifies a dissatisfier the system must possess in order to be successfully introduced to the market.  
Satisfiers: A requirement specifies a satisfier if the customers consciously demand the associated property. Satisfiers of the system specify the degree of satisfaction of the customer. An increase in the number of satisfiers usually leads to increased customer satisfaction.  
Delighters: A requirement specifies a delighter if the customers do not consciously demand the defined system property, or the customers do not expect the implementation of the property. Customer satisfaction increases exponentially by implementing delighters. 
Three Level Scale  
 
 
MOSCOW Technique  
Instead of numbers, this method uses four priority groups: MUST have, SHOULD have, COULD have, and WON'T have. The acronym represents the following: Department of Software Engineering  2025 Department of Software Engineering  2025 
MUST (Mandatory) 
SHOULD (Of high priority) 
COULD (Preferred but not necessary) 
WOULD (Can be postponed and suggested for future execution) 
Bubble Sort Technique  
To prioritize requirements using bubble sort, you take two requirements and compare them with each other. If you find out that one requirement should have greater priority over the other, you swap them accordingly. You then continue in this fashion until the very last requirement is properly sorted. The result is a list of requirements that are ranked.

LAB 13: Traceability of requirements Department of Software Engineering  2025 Department of Software Engineering  2025 
Objective  
The objective of the lab is to get an understanding of requirements traceability and applying requirements traceability techniques 
Theoretical Description 
Requirements management comprises purposefully assigning attributes to requirements, An important aspect of requirements management is ensuring the traceability of requirements. The traceability of a requirement is the ability to trace the requirements over the course of the entire life cycle of the system.tracebility of requirement has following objectives 
Traceability of requirements allows verifying whether a requirement has been implemented in the system, i.e., if the requirement has been implemented through a system property. 
Traceability of requirements allows for the identification of  gold-plated solutions of the developed system 
Traceability of requirements allows for the analysis of effects during change management 
Types of requirements traceability 
 
Requirements traceability information can be represented in different ways. The most common approaches to representing traceability are simple textual references, hyperlinks, and trace matrices and trace graphs Department of Software Engineering  2025   Representation of requirements traceability  Department of Software Engineering  2025   Representation of requirements traceability  
Text-Based References and Hyperlinks 
 This simple way to represent traceability information of a requirement consists of annotating the target artifact as a textual reference in the requirement (initial artifact) or to establish a hyperlink between the initial artifact and the target artifact. When linking artifacts, different types of hyperlinks with specific link semantics can be used. 
Trace Matrices  
Another common technique for representing and documenting traceability information between requirements as well as between requirements and previous and posterior artifacts in the development process are trace matrices. The rows in a trace matrix contain the initial artifacts (requirements). In the columns, the target artifacts (e.g., sources of requirements, development artifacts, requirements) are represented. If a trace link exists between an initial artifact in row n and a target artifact in column m, cell (n, m) is marked in the trace matrix. 
 
 
For example,  Department of Software Engineering  2025 Department of Software Engineering  2025 
 
Trace graphs 
A trace graph is a graph in which all nodes represent artifacts and all edges represent relationships between artifacts. The distinction between different artifacts and types of traceability can be realized by means of assigning different attributes to the nodes and edges of the graph for example

Post RS traceability relations and traceability between requirements

LAB 14: Requirement configuration management and change management Department of Software Engineering  2025 Department of Software Engineering  2025 
Objective  
The objectives of this lab is to understand the purpose of configuration management and how to handle change management. The techniques used to manage requirement changes and understand the tasks performed by change control board 
Theoretical description 
A requirements configuration consists of a set of requirements with the additional condition that each selected requirement is present in the requirements configuration with exactly one version, identified by the version number. Managing configurations of requirements can be described in two dimensions. In the product dimension, configuration management deals with individual requirements within the requirements base (foundation). In the version dimension, configuration management considers the various change states as part of version management within the product dimension.  
Figure shown below illustrates both dimensions of configuration management of requirements. On the requirements axis, requirements are represented. On the version axis, the different versions of the requirements are depicted 
 
 
A configuration of requirements has the following properties:  Department of Software Engineering  2025 Department of Software Engineering  2025 
Logical connection: The requirements contained in a configuration are directly logically connected to one another, i.e., a goal-oriented grouping of the requirements to a common configuration has been performed.  
Consistency: The requirements contained in a configuration do not contradict one another, i.e., the configuration contains requirements that are contradiction free in their respective version.  
Unique identification: A configuration has a unique identifier (ID) which can be used to uniquely identify the configuration.  
Immutable: A configuration defines a certain, immutable state of the specification. If requirements of a configuration are changed, a new version of the requirements and potentially of the configuration is the result.  
Basis for rollbacks: If changes of requirements must be undone, configurations offer the ability to roll back requirements to a specific version within a configuration. Therefore, a consistent state of the specification can be maintained 
Change control board 
Over the course of the system life cycle, it is necessary to channel change requests for requirements and define a structured process that will lead to a justified decision about whether a change request is approved and how itis approved. Changes can pertain to individual requirements (e.g., redefining a requirement) or the entire requirements document. The evaluation of requirements changes, as well as the decision about performing the change, is usually the responsibility of a change control board. It is responsible for following tasks 
Estimate the effort for performing the change (potentially commission a third party with an effort analysis).  
Evaluate change requests, e.g., with respect to the effort/benefit ratio.  
Define requirement changes or define new requirements on the basis of change requests.  
Decide about acceptance or rejection of change requests.  
 
Classify incoming change requests.  Department of Software Engineering  2025 Department of Software Engineering  2025 
Prioritize accepted change requests.  
Assign accepted change requests to change projects 
The change Request 
A change request should contain the following information:  
Identifier: The identifier makes it possible to uniquely identify a change request at any point during the life cycle of the system.  
Title: The title summarizes the key concern of the change request in one brief statement.  
Description: The description documents the requirement change as precisely as possible. It can contain information on the effect of the changes as well.  
Justification: The most important reasons as to why the change is necessary are listed here.  
Date filed: The date at which the change request was filed.  
Applicant: The name of the person that issued the change request.  
Priority (in the applicant’s opinion): The importance of the change request according to the applicant’s opinion. 
Lab Tasks 
Create a configuration management plan of your project 
Identify the changes that needs to be done in the project and prepare a change request form for each of the highlighted change

Open Ended Lab (OEL) Department of Software Engineering  2025 Department of Software Engineering  2025 
         
Course: Software Requirement Engineering                                                 Total Marks: 15                           
 
OEL Title: Designing Requirements Documentation for a Community Help Platform 
 
OEL Level: 2 Objectives: 
To apply requirements engineering principles by identifying, analyzing, and documenting requirements for a proposed real-world software system. 
Background Information: 
Requirements engineering is the process of discovering, analyzing, and specifying what a system should do. It includes both functional and non-functional requirements, constraints, and various documentation formats. In real-world projects, there is rarely one "right way" to define system behavior, and the role of a requirements engineer is to clarify stakeholder needs into clear, structured documentation. 
Problem: 
Suppose you have been hired as a requirements engineer by a non-profit organization to help design a Community Help Platform — a web and mobile-based application that connects volunteers with people who need help within a local community. 
The platform should support the following basic ideas: 
People can post help requests for tasks like picking up groceries, getting tutoring, or walking a pet. 
Volunteers can browse and accept requests. 
The system should enable safe and secure communication between parties. 
As the requirements engineer, your task is to analyze this scenario and produce a clear set of initial requirements documentation. You are free to decide which methods and formats to use for capturing and representing these requirements. 
 
Requirements: 
Submit a structured solution that includes: 
User Requirements 
Elicit at least five key user needs or expectations. 
 
Use your choice of technique (e.g., user stories, scenarios, brainstorming, etc.). Department of Software Engineering  2025 Department of Software Engineering  2025 
System Requirements 
Translate the user needs into at least five corresponding system requirements. 
Documentation:  
Present your requirements documentation in a clear, organized, and appropriate format of your choice that effectively communicates your understanding and analysis of the problem. 
Constraints 
Identify and briefly describe at least three constraints that the system should respect (technical, business, or legal). 
Non-Functional Requirements 
List at least two non-functional requirements, such as performance, usability, or security. 
Note: Creativity, justification of choices, and real-world reasoning will be a major part of the evaluation. Multiple approaches are acceptable.

Name: Abdul Samad 
Program: BSSE Group A 
Semester: 5th 
Date: September 16, 2026
Lab Task 2 - Report
*---------------------------------------------*Scenario: Online Food Delivery System
Problem Statement
Customers browse restaurants and place orders. Restaurants receive orders and update order status. Delivery riders receive delivery requests and update delivery status. A payment service processes online payments. An administrator manages users, restaurants, and complaints.
Extracted Requirements
R1: Customers must be able to browse restaurants/menus and place orders.
R2: Customers must be able to pay for orders online.
R3: Restaurants must be able to receive orders and update order status.
R4: Delivery riders must be able to receive delivery requests and update delivery status.
R5: The system must communicate with a payment service to process payments.
R6: An administrator must be able to manage users, restaurants, and complaints.
Identify External Entities
The following entities are outside the boundary of the Online Food Delivery System but interact with it:
External Entity | Why External? | Major Interaction
Customer | A person using the system, not an internal software component. | Requests restaurant/menu information, places orders, makes payments, receives order status.
Restaurant | An independent business external to the software system. | Receives new orders; sends order status updates.
Delivery Rider | A person outside the software system who fulfils deliveries. | Receives delivery requests; sends delivery status updates.
Payment Service | A separate external paymentprocessing service. | Receives payment requests; sends payment confirmation.
Administrator | A person managing the platform, not an internal component. | Manages users, restaurants, and complaints.
Identify Major Information Flow

External Entity  | Information Sent to System | Information Received | Related Requirements
Customer | Browse request, order placement request, payment info | Restaurant/menu list, order confirmation, order status updates | R1, R2
Restaurant | Order status update | New order details | R3
Delivery Rider | Delivery status update | Delivery request | R4
Payment Service | Payment confirmation | Payment request | R5
Administrator | Manage users / restaurants / complaints | Management confirmation / records | R6
Context Diagram
The context diagram below treats the entire Online Food Delivery System as one unit. Customer, Restaurant, Delivery Rider, Payment Service, and Administrator remain outside the system boundary. Internal modules are intentionally not shown here.

Explanation
The central node represents the complete software system.
Customer, Restaurant, Delivery Rider, Payment Service, and Administrator are external entities.
Flows are labeled with meaningful information (e.g., "Order Request / Login") rather than generic terms such as "data".
The diagram does not show databases, screens, classes, APIs, or internal modules.
Payment Service is external because payment processing is performed by a separate service, not by the ordering platform itself.
Major Internal Modules

Internal Module | Responsibility
User Management | Manages customer, restaurant, and rider accounts and profiles.
Restaurant Management | Maintains restaurant listings, menus, and availability.
Order Management | Processes order placement and coordinates order status across modules.
Delivery Management | Assigns delivery requests to riders and tracks delivery status.
Payment Management | Handles payment requests and communicates with the external Payment Service.
Notification Management | Sends status updates and alerts to customers, restaurants, and riders.
Complaint/Admin Management | Allows the administrator to manage users, restaurants, and complaints.
System Diagram
The system diagram opens the system boundary and shows the major internal modules and their relationships. It remains high-level and does not describe source code classes or individual database fields.


Explanation
Order Management is the central coordinating module, connecting to Restaurant Management, Delivery Management, and Payment Management.
Notification Management supports Order Management and Delivery Management by sending status updates.
User Management handles account-related requests from Customers and feeds into Order Management.
Complaint/Admin Management gives the Administrator control over User Management and Restaurant Management (e.g approving/removing restaurants, resolving complaints).
Restaurant Management, Delivery Management, and Payment Management each interface directly with their corresponding external entity (Restaurant, Delivery Rider, Payment Service).
Context Diagram vs. System Diagram
Aspect | Context Diagram | System Diagram
Perspective | External / boundary view | Internal high-level view
System representation | One complete system | Major internal modules
External entities | Shown | Shown where useful for interaction 
 |  | context
Internal modules | Not shown | Shown
Main purpose | Define boundary and external interactions | Explain major internal organization
Level of detail | Very high level | More detailed, but still conceptual
Requirement to Diagram Traceability
Requirement | Context Diagram Evidence | System Diagram Evidence
R1 Browse & order | Customer <-> System (Order Request / Login) | User Management -> Order Management
R2 Online payment | System <-> Payment Service | Order Management -> Payment Management
R3 Restaurant order/status | System <-> Restaurant | Order Management <-> Restaurant Management
R4 Delivery request/status | System <-> Delivery Rider | Order Management / Notification Management <-> Delivery Management
R5 Payment processing | System <-> Payment Service | Payment Management <-> Payment Service
R6 Admin manages users/restaurants/complaints | Administrator <-> System | Complaint/Admin Management <-> User Management, Restaurant Management
Ambiguities and Assumptions
Ambiguities
The problem statement does not specify whether Notification Management is a requirement or an implementation choice, it was added as a supporting module for order status updates.
The scope of "complaints" is not defined , it is unclear whether complaints can be raised by customers, restaurants, or riders, or all three.
Assumptions
Payment Service is assumed to be a separate external system.
Restaurants are assumed to have some interface (app/portal) to receive orders and update status, since the requirement states they "receive orders and update order status".
Administrator is assumed to be a single internal role with access to Complaint/Admin Management, rather than an external organization.

14. Lab Review / Presentation Questions and Answers

Why did you classify this entity as external?

Student, Hostel Office, University Authentication System. and University Finance System are outside me

software being modeled. first two are users/organizationa/ roles. while me latter two are separate external

Why is this component inside the system boundary?

The intemal rnodules are responsibüities that the proposed University Hostel Management System itself

performs, such as roan rnanagernent, applicatms, anocation, fees. complaints. remrds, and reporting.

What requirement supports this information flow?

Each flow is traced to RI—R9. For example. room availability is by R2, appåcations by R3,

authentzatbn by RI/R8, and fee verification by R5tR9

What happens if the external service becomes unavailable?

The system should not confirm an operation that depends on the unavailable service. It should report that

authenbcation or payment verificabon is temporarily unavailable and allow the user to retry-

Which requirement was ambiguous?

The original proposed scenario does not specify allocation priority, payment processing details, complaint-

resolution rules, or duplicate-application rules. These were documented as assumptionx

What assumption did your group make?

We assumed that the Hostel Office defines allocation rules and that the Finance System handles or verifies

payment informatbn externany.

Why did you choose these internal modules?

They map directly to the main responsibilities in the scenario: authentication, room avÜbdity,

appbcabons/albcatim, fees, complaints, records, and administration/reportÉ4

Could two modules be combined? Why?

Room & Avadabdity ManagetTEnt and Application & Allocation could be combined in a very srnall system, but

they are kept separate because rmm availability and applicatiowalbocatjon are distinct responsibdltjes.

Does the system diagram support all major functions in the scenario?

SOFTWARE REQUIREMENTS ENGINEERING (SRE)LABORATORY MANUAL
Generating System and Context Diagrams
A Practical Requirements Modeling Exercise
Lab Overview
This laboratory exercise introduces students to practical requirements modeling through system and context diagrams. Students will convert a textual problem statement into visual models by identifying the system boundary, external entities, information flows, major internal components, ambiguities, and assumptions. The emphasis is on requirements analysis and validation rather than simply drawing diagrams.
Lab Information
Lab Title | Generating System and Context Diagrams
Course | Software Requirements Engineering (SRE)
Duration | Approximately 2 hours / 120 minutes
Lab Type | Hands-on requirements analysis, modeling, peer review, and presentation
Recommended Group Size | 3–4 students

Learning Objectives
By the end of the lab, students should be able to:
Identify the system boundary from a textual requirements statement.
Identify users, organizations, external applications, devices, and other external entities.
Identify major inputs, outputs, and information/data flows.
Construct a context diagram showing the system and its external interactions.
Decompose a system into appropriate major internal modules/components.
Construct a high-level system diagram showing relationships among internal components.
Distinguish external entities from internal system components.
Identify ambiguities, assumptions, and missing requirements.
Validate diagrams against the original requirements.
Justify modeling decisions during peer review and presentation.
Conceptual Foundation
Context Diagram
A context diagram presents the system from an external perspective. The complete target system is represented as one central system/process, while external entities are placed outside the system boundary. Labeled information or data flows show what enters and leaves the system.
System as one unit
System boundary
External entities/actors
Major information or data flows
A context diagram should normally avoid internal modules, database tables, algorithms, classes, individual screens, and implementation details.
System Diagram
For this laboratory, the system diagram provides an internal high-level view. It decomposes the system into major functional modules/components and shows their principal relationships. It should remain at an appropriate abstraction level and should not become a detailed source-code or database design.
User Management
Order/Transaction Management
Authentication/Authorization
Payment Management
Notification Management
Reporting
Requirement Engineering Connection
The activity follows the requirements engineering principle that models should be derived from requirements. Students should first analyze the problem statement, identify entities and interactions, document assumptions, and then create diagrams. Each important diagram element should be traceable to a requirement or an explicitly documented assumption.
Required Tools and Resources
Computer/laptop for each student or group.
Diagramming software such as diagrams.net (Draw.io), Microsoft Visio, PowerPoint, Lucidchart, or equivalent.
The scenario supplied by the instructor.
Word processor/PDF editor for the final report.
Internet connection if an online diagramming tool is selected.
Workflow
Problem Statement → Requirements → External Entities → Data Flows → Context Diagram → Internal Modules → System Diagram → Validation
Detailed Lab Procedure
Identify the System Boundary
State exactly what software system is being modeled and distinguish what belongs inside from what remains external.
Identify External Entities
List users, organizations, external applications, services, devices, or other systems that exchange information with the target system.

Identify Inputs and Outputs
For every external entity, identify what information is sent to the system and what information is received from it.
Construct the Context Diagram
Represent the complete system as one central system/process. Place external entities around it and connect them using meaningful, directional, labeled flows.
Review the Context Diagram
Check completeness, boundary correctness, labeling, direction, and traceability to the scenario.
Identify Major Internal Modules
Move inside the system boundary and identify approximately 5–8 major functional modules/components.
Construct the System Diagram
Show the major internal modules and their principal relationships/interactions. Avoid excessive implementation detail.
Record Ambiguities and Assumptions
Document unclear requirements and state any assumptions made to proceed.
Peer Review
Exchange diagrams with another group and use the review checklist.
Presentation
Each group explains its system, diagrams, assumptions, and one important modeling decision.
Primary Practice Scenario
University Course Registration System
Students use an online University Course Registration System to view available courses, register for courses, drop courses, and view their registered courses. Teachers can view students enrolled in their courses. The Academic/Examination Office manages course offerings and registration rules. The system communicates with a University Authentication System to verify user identities.
Before drawing, ask:
Who are the external entities?
What information does each entity send?
What information does each entity receive?
Which functions belong inside the system?
Which component is external even though the system depends on it?
Which requirements are ambiguous or require clarification?
Student Analysis Worksheet
Complete this analysis before drawing the context diagram.
External Entity | Information Sent | Information Received | Notes / Assumptions
 |  |  | 
 |  |  | 
 |  |  | 
 |  |  | 
 |  |  | 
 |  |  | 

Context Diagram Requirements
Represent the complete target system as one central system/process.
Show all major external entities.
Use meaningful, directional information/data flows.
Clearly label every flow.
Maintain a clear system boundary.
Do not include internal modules or detailed implementation.
Ensure major interactions are supported by the requirements.
System Diagram Requirements
Show major internal modules/components.
Use meaningful names based on system responsibilities.
Show principal relationships/interactions.
Maintain a high-level abstraction.
Avoid database columns, individual UI controls, and source-code functions.
Ensure modules collectively support the functions described in the scenario.
Alternative Student Scenarios
Online Food Delivery System
Customers browse restaurants and place orders. Restaurants receive orders and update order status. Delivery riders receive delivery requests and update delivery status. A payment service processes online payments. An administrator manages users, restaurants, and complaints.
Library Management System
Students search for books, borrow and return books, and view borrowing history. Librarians manage books, members, and borrowing records. A notification service may send overdue reminders.
Online Examination System
Students log in, view available examinations, attempt questions, and submit answers. Teachers create examinations and view results. An administrator manages users and examination settings.
Hospital Management System
Patients register and book appointments. Doctors view appointments and patient information. Receptionists manage schedules. A laboratory provides test results and a pharmacy manages prescribed medicines.
E-Commerce System
Customers browse products, place orders, make payments, and track deliveries. Sellers manage products and orders. A payment gateway processes transactions and a delivery service handles shipment.
Bus Ticket Reservation System
Passengers search routes, select seats, book tickets, and cancel reservations. Operators manage routes, schedules, buses, and seats. A payment service processes online payments.
Assessment Rubrics

Information/data flows | 2 | Flows are relevant, directional, meaningful, and traceable.
Context diagram | 2 | Correct system boundary, one high-level system representation, appropriate interactions.
System diagram | 2 | Appropriate internal modules and meaningful relationships at suitable abstraction.
Requirements analysis & presentation | 2 | Assumptions/ambiguities documented and modeling decisions clearly justified.
Total | 10 | 

Questions:

What assumption did your group make?

Submission Guidelines
Submit one Word report containing all required deliverables. Diagrams must be readable, consistently labeled, and clearly associated with the assigned system. Students should include group/member information as required by the instructor.

Scenario: University Course Registration System
 Problem Statement
Students use an online University Course Registration System to view available courses, register for courses, drop courses, and view their registered courses. Teachers can view the students enrolled in their courses. The Academic/Examination Office manages course offerings and registration rules. The system communicates with a University Authentication System to verify user identities.
Extract the Requirements
R1: Students must be able to authenticate and access the registration system.
R2: Students must be able to view available courses.
R3: Students must be able to register for courses.
R4: Students must be able to drop registered courses.
R5: Students must be able to view their registered courses.
R6: Teachers must be able to view students enrolled in their courses.
R7: The Academic/Examination Office must be able to manage course offerings and registration rules.
R8: The system must communicate with the University Authentication System for identity verification.
Identify External Entities
The following entities are outside the boundary of the Course Registration System but interact with it:
External Entity | Why External? | Major Interaction
Student | A person using the system, not an internal software component. | Requests course information, registration, dropping, and registered-course information.
Teacher | A person outside the software system. | Requests information about students enrolled in courses.
Academic/Examination Office | An external organizational role responsible for academic administration. | Provides course offerings and registration rules; receives management information.
University Authentication System | A separate external software service. | Verifies user identity/authentication.

Identify Major Information Flow
External Entity | Information Sent to System | Information Received | Related Requirements
Student | Login credentials; course registration request; course-drop request; course search/view request | Authentication result; available courses; registration confirmation; registered-course list; drop confirmation | R1–R5
Teacher | Enrollment information request | Enrolled-student information | R6
Academic/Examination Office | Course offerings; registration rules | Course-management/registration information | R7
University Authentication System | Authentication result / identity verification response | Authentication/identity verification request | R8

Context Diagram
The context diagram below treats the entire Course Registration System as one unit. Notice that Student, Teacher, Academic/Examination Office, and University Authentication System remain outside the system. Internal modules such as Registration Management or Course Management are intentionally NOT shown here.
                 ┌──────────────────────┐                 │       Student        │                 └──────────┬───────────┘                            │              Registration / Drop / View Requests                            │                            ▼        ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐        │                                        │        │     UNIVERSITY COURSE REGISTRATION     │        │                 SYSTEM                 │        │                                        │        └────────────────────────────────────────┘             ▲             ▲              ▲             │             │              │       Course Lists,   Enrolled       Course /       Confirmations   Students       Rule Info             │             │              │   ┌─────────┴───┐    ┌────┴─────┐  ┌────┴─────────────────┐   │   Student   │    │ Teacher  │  │ Academic/Examination │   └─────────────┘    └──────────┘  │        Office         │                                     └───────────────────────┘                  Authentication Request                         ───────►              ┌────────────────────────────┐              │ University Authentication │              │          System            │              └────────────────────────────┘                         ◄───────                    Verification Result

C.D Explanation
The central box represents the complete software system.
Student, Teacher, Academic/Examination Office, and University Authentication System are external entities.
Flows are labeled with meaningful information rather than generic words such as 'data'.
The context diagram does not show databases, screens, classes, APIs, or internal modules.
The Authentication System is external because the scenario states that identity verification is performed by a separate system.
Major Internal Modules
Internal Module | Responsibility
Authentication & Access Control | Handles login/access requests and communicates with the external authentication service.
Course Catalog Management | Maintains and provides information about available courses.
Registration Management | Processes course registration requests and applies registration rules.
Course Drop Management | Processes requests to drop registered courses.
Enrollment Management | Maintains and provides enrollment information for courses.
Academic Administration | Allows authorized academic staff to manage course offerings and registration rules.
Student Records / Registration History | Maintains relevant registered-course information and history.

System diagram
The system diagram now opens the system boundary and shows the major internal modules. It is intentionally high-level: it does not describe source-code classes or individual database fields.
                     ┌──────────────────────────────┐                     │ University Authentication     │                     │          System               │                     └──────────────┬───────────────┘                                    │                                    ▼                    ┌──────────────────────────────┐                    │ Authentication & Access       │                    │          Control              │                    └──────────────┬───────────────┘                                   │              ┌────────────────────┼─────────────────────┐              │                    │                     │              ▼                    ▼                     ▼   ┌──────────────────┐  ┌────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────┐   │ Course Catalog    │  │ Registration       │  │ Course Drop      │   │ Management        │  │ Management         │  │ Management       │   └────────┬─────────┘  └──────────┬─────────┘  └────────┬─────────┘            │                       │                     │            └──────────────┬────────┴─────────────┬──────┘                           ▼                      ▼                 ┌──────────────────┐   ┌──────────────────────┐                 │ Enrollment       │   │ Student Records /    │                 │ Management       │   │ Registration History │                 └────────┬─────────┘   └──────────────────────┘                          │                          ▼                 ┌──────────────────────┐                 │ Academic             │                 │ Administration       │                 │ (Courses & Rules)    │                 └──────────────────────┘ External interactions: Student → Authentication / Course Catalog / Registration / Course Drop Teacher → Enrollment Management Academic Office → Academic Administration
S.D Explanation
Authentication & Access Control receives authentication-related requests and interacts with the external University Authentication System.
Course Catalog Management provides available-course information.
Registration Management processes course registration requests and uses course/enrollment information.
Course Drop Management handles dropping requests and updates registration-related information.
Enrollment Management provides course enrollment information, particularly for teachers.
Academic Administration supports management of course offerings and registration rules.
Student Records / Registration History represents the internal responsibility for registered-course information and history.
Context Diagram vs. System Diagram
Aspect | Context Diagram | System Diagram
Perspective | External / boundary view | Internal high-level view
System representation | One complete system | Major internal modules
External entities | Shown | May be shown where useful for interaction context
Internal modules | Not shown | Shown
Main purpose | Define boundary and external interactions | Explain major internal organization
Level of detail | Very high level | More detailed, but still conceptual

Requirement to Diagram Traceability
Requirement | Context Diagram Evidence | System Diagram Evidence
R1 Authentication | Student ↔ System; System ↔ Authentication System | Authentication & Access Control ↔ Authentication System
R2 View courses | Student ↔ System | Student-facing interaction with Course Catalog Management
R3 Register courses | Student ↔ System | Registration Management
R4 Drop courses | Student ↔ System | Course Drop Management
R5 View registered courses | Student ↔ System | Student Records / Registration History
R6 Teacher views enrolled students | Teacher ↔ System | Enrollment Management
R7 Academic office manages courses/rules | Academic Office ↔ System | Academic Administration
R8 External identity verification | System ↔ Authentication System | Authentication & Access Control ↔ Authentication System

Takeaway
The same requirement can appear at different abstraction levels in the two diagrams.
The context diagram is not a detailed architecture diagram.
The system diagram should not simply repeat the context diagram; it opens the system and exposes its major responsibilities.
An external system remains external even when an internal module communicates with it.
A diagram element should have a reason: it should be supported by a requirement or documented assumption.
Good diagrams use meaningful names and avoid unexplained arrows.
Questions:
Why is Student outside the system boundary?
Why is Registration Management inside the system?
Why is the University Authentication System external?
Why is 'Registration Request' a better flow name than simply 'Data'?
Why should the database not normally appear in this context diagram?
Why do we need a separate system diagram after creating the context diagram?
Which requirement justifies Enrollment Management?
What would change if the university developed its own authentication module instead of using a separate authentication system?

Software Requirements Engineering – Lab Report
Sources of Requirements + Kano Model — University Course Registration System
Group: Hudaibia, Sarah Arif, Eshaal Nazir, Abdul Samad
Submitted to: Sir Fahim Muhammad Khan      Date: 24 Sept 2026
1. What we did
For this lab we had to find out where the requirements for a new university course registration system should come from and then use the Kano Model to check how students feel about some possible features of it. We picked 8 sources, listed 10 candidate features, made a Kano questionnaire out of them, sent it out, and got 40 responses back. Below is everything we found.
2. Sources of requirements (8)
Source | Example | What we get from it
Students | The people who will actually use the system | What they need, what annoys them now
Registrar office | Registration staff | Rules, approvals, policies
Faculty | Course instructors | Prerequisites, seat limits
IT staff | University IT department | Security, servers, technical limits
Current system | The old manual process | What already works, what doesn't
Academic policies | University rules and deadlines | What the system must follow
Watching students register | Observing registration week | Real problems people run into
Survey | Our Kano questionnaire | What students actually want most
3. Candidate features (10)
These are the 10 features we picked, based on the sources above, and later put into our survey.
No. | Feature
1 | Search courses by code/title/department
2 | Show remaining seats
3 | Registration confirmation
4 | SMS/email notification
5 | Automatic course recommendations
6 | Dark mode
7 | Download timetable as PDF
8 | Remember selected courses
9 | Save data if network drops
10 | Fast response at peak times
4. The Kano questionnaire
For each of the 10 features above we made two questions, one asking how the student would feel if the feature WAS there, and one asking how they'd feel if it was NOT there. Both used the same 5 answers: I like it / I expect it / I am neutral / I can tolerate it / I dislike it. Here are the actual question pairs we used:
Feature | Functional question | Dysfunctional question
Course search | How would you feel if you could search courses by code/title/dept? | How would you feel if you could NOT search courses this way?
Seat display | How would you feel if the system showed remaining seats? | How would you feel if it did NOT show remaining seats?
Registration confirmation | How would you feel if you got a confirmation after registering? | How would you feel if you did NOT get any confirmation?
SMS/email notification | How would you feel if you got SMS/email updates about registration? | How would you feel if you did NOT get any such updates?
Course recommendations | How would you feel if the system recommended courses to you? | How would you feel if it did NOT recommend anything?
Dark mode | How would you feel if the system had a dark mode option? | How would you feel if it did NOT have dark mode?
Download timetable | How would you feel if you could download your timetable as PDF? | How would you feel if you could NOT download it?
Remember courses | How would you feel if it remembered your picks before you submit? | How would you feel if it did NOT remember your picks?
Data preservation | How would you feel if your data was safe during a network drop? | How would you feel if your data was lost during a network drop?
Fast peak response | How would you feel if the system stayed fast during rush hours? | How would you feel if it got slow during rush hours?
We built this as a Google Form titled "Kano Analysis — University Course Registration System", tested it ourselves first, then sent it out to students.
Form link: https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSf-5ZQl_5JUhBtiqAMdy_f3jSNCsk0-UHsZsZPPcJL35pUbOw/viewform
5. How we classified answers
We used the standard Kano table below to turn each pair of answers into one letter (A/O/M/I/R/Q). This was done in a spreadsheet, not by hand, for all 40 responses. Our raw responses and the full classification of every single answer are in a separate Excel file (Kano_Analysis_Full.xlsx) attached along with this report.
Have it \ Don't have it | Like | Expect | Neutral | Tolerate | Dislike
Like | Q | A | A | A | O
Expect | R | I | I | I | M
Neutral | R | I | I | I | M
Tolerate | R | I | I | I | M
Dislike | R | R | R | R | Q
6. Results (n = 40)
A few people skipped a question or two here and there, so those specific answers were left out and not counted for that one feature.
Feature | A | O | M | I | R | Q | Dominant
Course search | 15 | 11 | 1 | 8 | 0 | 4 | Attractive
Seat display | 12 | 9 | 4 | 9 | 0 | 4 | Attractive
Registration confirmation | 5 | 12 | 5 | 10 | 2 | 4 | One-dimensional
SMS/email notification | 9 | 9 | 2 | 13 | 1 | 4 | Indifferent
Course recommendations | 8 | 8 | 1 | 12 | 3 | 4 | Indifferent
Dark mode | 6 | 8 | 1 | 13 | 5 | 6 | Indifferent
Download timetable | 8 | 11 | 5 | 7 | 1 | 6 | One-dimensional
Remember courses | 9 | 8 | 3 | 10 | 3 | 4 | Indifferent
Data preservation | 5 | 8 | 3 | 10 | 3 | 8 | Indifferent
Fast peak response | 7 | 12 | 5 | 9 | 1 | 5 | One-dimensional

7. What the results mean
Course search and the seat display came out as Attractive, students like having them but won't get too mad if they're basic, though for this system we'd still build both early since the whole app is built around them. Registration confirmation, downloading the timetable, and fast response at busy times all came out One-dimensional, so the better we do these, the happier students are, and the worse we do them, the more they complain. Everything else, notifications, recommendations, dark mode, remembering courses, saving data during network issues, came out mostly Indifferent, students don't care much either way.
Questionable example: "Save data if network drops" had the most Questionable answers (8 out of 40). We think it's because the question describes a specific situation and not everyone imagined the same thing when answering both parts, so their answers ended up contradicting each other.
Indifferent example: Dark mode had the most Indifferent answers (13 out of 40). Makes sense, it's just a look/theme thing and has nothing to do with actually registering for a class, so most people don't really care if it's there or not.
8. Does this decide what we build first?
Not on its own. Kano only tells us how students feel about a feature, it doesn't tell us how much time, money, or effort that feature needs, and it doesn't account for things like server limits or approval processes that the registrar or IT team have to deal with. So even though course search came out "just" Attractive, we'd still build it early since the whole system depends on it. Registration confirmation and fast response at peak times came out One-dimensional, so these need to be done well since students will notice immediately if they're slow or broken. Something like dark mode being Indifferent means it's fine to leave for later, or drop it completely if the team is short on time, since it won't really change how satisfied students are either way. Basically, Kano tells us how people feel, but we still need to think about cost and effort before deciding what actually gets built first.
