SOFTWARE REQUIREMENTS ENGINEERING
Laboratory Exercise
Identify Sources of Requirements and Apply the Kano Model
Case Study: University Course Registration System

Item | Details
Course | Software Requirements Engineering (SRE)
Lab Type | Practical / Requirements Elicitation & Analysis
Recommended Tools | Google Forms + Google Sheets
Optional Tool | Miro for stakeholder/source mapping
Estimated Duration | 2–3 hours
Student Work | Individual or groups of 3–4


Lab Overview:
This laboratory exercise introduces students to two practical requirements-engineering tasks: (1) identifying different sources from which software requirements can be obtained, and (2) using the Kano Model to understand how users perceive candidate features. Students will work with a University Course Registration System, collect structured feedback, classify responses, and prepare a requirements analysis summary.
Tools Required:
Tool | Purpose | Lab Use
Google Forms | Online data collection | Create the Kano questionnaire and collect responses.
Google Sheets | Analysis | Store raw responses, classify features, summarize results, and create charts.
Google Drive | Sharing/storage | Store and share the form and spreadsheet.
Miro (optional) | Visual collaboration | Map stakeholders and requirement sources before questionnaire design.

Recommended demonstration: use Google Forms + Google Sheets for the complete lab. If only one tool is available, Google Sheets can support the entire analysis workflow.
Case Study:
A university plans to develop a new University Course Registration System. The existing process may require students to check course availability manually, visit offices, or use separate communication channels for confirmation. The proposed system should support course search, availability checking, registration, confirmation, and registration management.
Students, instructors, registrar/academic staff, department personnel, and IT staff may all be stakeholders. Your task is to identify where requirements should come from and then investigate how users value possible system features using the Kano Model.
Sources of Requirements:
Identify at least eight relevant requirement sources for the case study.
Source | Example | Information Obtained
Students / End Users | Students registering for courses | Goals, problems, usability needs, preferences
Registrar / Academic Office | Registration staff | Rules, approval process, policies
Faculty / Instructors | Course instructors | Prerequisites, capacity, instructor constraints
IT / System Administrators | University IT staff | Security, infrastructure, integration, technical constraints
Existing System / Process | Current registration workflow | Current functions, limitations, data, workarounds
Documents / Policies | Academic regulations | Mandatory rules, deadlines, eligibility
Observation | Observe registration activity | Actual behavior, interruptions, workarounds
Interviews / Meetings | Stakeholder discussions | Detailed needs, concerns, exceptions
Surveys | Student/staff survey | Opinions and patterns across larger groups
External / Comparable Systems | Other universities | Common features and alternative approaches

Develop Candidate Requirements:
From your identified sources, create at least 10 candidate requirements/features. Each item should be specific enough to evaluate.
No. | Candidate Feature | Possible Source | Problem Addressed
1 | Search courses by code, title, or department | Students | Finding courses quickly
2 | Display remaining seats | Students / Registrar | Avoiding unavailable-course attempts
3 | Registration confirmation | Students / Registrar | Providing clear status
4 | SMS/email notification | Students / University | Improving communication
5 | Automatic course recommendations | Students / Faculty | Helping students discover courses
6 | Dark mode | Students | Display preference
7 | Download timetable as PDF | Students | Offline access
8 | Remember selected courses before final submission | Students | Reducing repeated work
9 | Preserve registration data during temporary network problems | Students / IT | Reducing data loss
10 | Fast response during peak registration | Students / IT | Reducing waiting time

Understand The Kano model
The Kano Model classifies features according to how their presence or absence affects user satisfaction. It helps distinguish expected basic features from performance-related and unexpected features.
Category | Meaning | Typical Reaction
Must-be (M) | Basic feature expected by users; absence can cause strong dissatisfaction. | Expected when present; unhappy when absent.
One-dimensional (O) | Satisfaction changes with the level of performance. | Better performance → more satisfaction.
Attractive (A) | Not necessarily expected, but presence can delight users. | Happy when present; absence usually causes little dissatisfaction.
Indifferent (I) | Little effect on satisfaction. | Little difference whether present or absent.
Reverse (R) | Some users prefer the feature not to exist. | Presence can reduce satisfaction.
Questionable (Q) | Paired answers are inconsistent or difficult to interpret. | Cannot reliably determine the respondent's category.

Important: Kano describes satisfaction behavior. It does not by itself determine final implementation priority. Cost, risk, business value, technical feasibility, security, legal requirements, and dependencies must also be considered.
Design the Kano Questionnaire 
For every selected feature, create two paired questions:
Type | Question Pattern | Example
Functional | How would you feel if the system HAD this feature? | How would you feel if the system provided automatic course recommendations?
Dysfunctional | How would you feel if the system DID NOT HAVE this feature? | How would you feel if the system did not provide automatic course recommendations?

Use the same five response options for both questions:
I like it
I expect it / It must be that way
I am neutral
I can tolerate it / I can live with it
I dislike it
Keep the wording simple. Do not use leading wording such as 'How useful is this excellent feature?' because it can bias the respondent.
Implement the Questionnaire in Google Forms:
1. Create a blank Google Form titled 'Kano Analysis — University Course Registration System'.
2. Add a short introduction explaining the purpose of the questionnaire.
3. For each selected feature, create one functional and one dysfunctional question.
4. Use identical response choices for both questions.
5. Keep respondent identification optional unless instructed otherwise.
6. Test the form before sharing it.
7. Collect responses from an appropriate group of intended users.
8. For a classroom demonstration, 15–30 responses are sufficient to practice the analysis; larger samples improve interpretation.
Analyze Responses in Google Sheets:
Link the Google Form to a Google Sheet. Keep the raw response sheet unchanged and create a separate analysis sheet.
Column | Purpose
Feature | Feature being evaluated
Functional Response | Response when the feature is present
Dysfunctional Response | Response when the feature is absent
Kano Category | A / O / M / I / R / Q
Notes | Unusual, ambiguous, or questionable cases

During the demonstration, manually classify a few response pairs first. Then show how the same logic can be applied consistently to many responses in the spreadsheet.
Understanding Questionable:
Questionable does not mean the requirement itself is bad. It means the respondent's pair of answers is inconsistent or difficult to interpret, so the response cannot be reliably assigned to a normal Kano category.
Functional | Dysfunctional | Interpretation
I like it | I like it | The respondent likes both having and not having the feature; inspect as potentially Questionable.
I dislike it | I dislike it | The respondent dislikes both states; inspect as potentially Questionable.

Do not confuse Questionable with Indifferent. Indifferent means the respondent genuinely does not care whether the feature exists. Questionable means the response pair does not provide a reliable basis for classification. If many Q responses occur for one feature, review the wording and respondent understanding.
Kano Evaluation matrix:
Use the following standard evaluation logic with the response order used in this lab.
Functional \ Dysfunctional | Like | Expect | Neutral | Tolerate | Dislike
Like | Q | A | A | A | O
Expect | R | I | I | I | M
Neutral | R | I | I | I | M
Tolerate | R | I | I | I | M
Dislike | R | R | R | R | Q

Start teaching with intuitive examples. For example, Like when present + Dislike when absent indicates a One-dimensional response. Like when present + Neutral/Expect/Tolerate when absent can indicate an Attractive response depending on the paired answers.
Summarize Results:
Count the number of A, O, M, I, R, and Q responses for each feature.
Feature | A | O | M | I | R | Q | Dominant
Course search |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
Available-seat display |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
Registration confirmation |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
SMS/email notification |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
Automatic recommendations |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
Dark mode |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
Download timetable |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
Remember selected courses |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
Data preservation |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
Fast peak-period response |  |  |  |  |  |  | 

Create at least one chart in Google Sheets showing the Kano results. A bar chart is recommended.
Use Kano Results for Requirements Discussion:
Kano findings should be combined with other requirements-engineering considerations. A feature with an Attractive classification is not automatically low priority, and a feature with a Must-be classification is not automatically the first item to implement without considering dependencies and constraints.
Feature | Possible Kano Result | Other Considerations
Registration confirmation | M / O | Business process, usability
Peak-period response | O | Performance and infrastructure cost
Course recommendations | A | Development effort and recommendation quality
Dark mode | I / A | Accessibility and user population
Security/privacy controls | May not be A | Risk, policy, compliance, legal obligations

Student Deliverables:
Requirements-source table containing at least eight sources.
At least 10 candidate requirements/features.
Completed Kano questionnaire with functional and dysfunctional questions.
Google Form link or screenshots.
Raw response spreadsheet.
Kano analysis/classification sheet.
Feature-by-feature Kano summary.
At least one chart.
Short interpretation of major findings.
Explanation of one Questionable and one Indifferent response pattern.
Short reflection on how Kano can support requirements prioritization.

SOFTWARE REQUIREMENTS ENGINEERING
Lab Report
Identifying Sources of Requirements and Applying the Kano Model
Case Study: University Course Registration System
Group Members
Hudaibia
Sarah Arif
Eshaal Nazir
Abdul Samad

Course: Software Requirements Engineering (SRE)
Submitted to: Sir Fahim Muhammad Khan
Date: September 24, 2026

1. Introduction
For this lab our group worked on two related tasks. First, we looked at where the requirements for a new software system should actually come from. Second, we used the Kano Model to understand how students feel about specific features of that system. The case study given to us was a university that wants to build a new Course Registration System. Right now, students have to check course availability manually, sometimes by visiting the registrar's office, and there is no single place where searching, registering, and confirming a registration happen together. Our job in this lab was to figure out who this system's requirements should come from, list out candidate features, build a Kano questionnaire for those features, collect responses from real students, and analyze what those responses tell us about which features actually matter.
2. Case Study Background
The university in this case study wants a system that lets students search for courses, check how many seats are left, register, receive confirmation, and manage their registration afterwards, all in one place. A system like this affects a lot of different people, not just students but also registrar staff, faculty, and the university's IT department, so before deciding what features to build, we needed to think about where the requirements for this system should come from and who should be asked.
3. Task 1: Sources of Requirements
As a group we identified the following eight sources of requirements for this system:
Source | Example | Information Obtained
Students / End Users | Students registering for courses | Goals, problems, usability needs, preferences
Registrar / Academic Office | Registration staff | Rules, approval process, policies
Faculty / Instructors | Course instructors | Prerequisites, capacity, instructor constraints
IT / System Administrators | University IT staff | Security, infrastructure, integration, technical constraints
Existing System / Process | Current registration workflow | Current functions, limitations, data, workarounds
Documents / Policies | Academic regulations | Mandatory rules, deadlines, eligibility
Observation | Observing students during registration week | Actual behaviour, interruptions, workarounds
Interviews / Meetings | Short discussions with registrar staff and a few instructors | Detailed needs, concerns, exceptions
Surveys | Kano questionnaire sent to students | Opinions and satisfaction patterns across a larger group
External / Comparable Systems | Registration portals of other universities | Common features and alternative approaches
Each of these sources gives a different kind of information. Students told us what they actually want and where the current process frustrates them, the registrar and faculty gave us the rules and constraints the system has to respect, and looking at the existing process and academic policies showed us what already works and what does not. We felt using this mix of sources, instead of only asking students, gave us a more complete picture before we started listing features.
4. Task 2: Candidate Requirements / Features
Based on the sources above, we listed the following ten candidate features for the new system. These are the same ten features we later tested with our Kano questionnaire.
No. | Candidate Feature | Possible Source | Problem Addressed
1 | Search courses by code, title, or department | Students | Finding courses quickly
2 | Display remaining seats | Students / Registrar | Avoiding attempts to register for full courses
3 | Registration confirmation | Students / Registrar | Providing clear status after registering
4 | SMS / email notification | Students / University | Improving communication
5 | Automatic course recommendations | Students / Faculty | Helping students discover suitable courses
6 | Dark mode | Students | Display preference
7 | Download timetable as PDF | Students | Offline access to schedule
8 | Remember selected courses before final submission | Students | Reducing repeated work
9 | Preserve registration data during a temporary network problem | Students / IT | Reducing data loss
10 | Fast response during peak registration | Students / IT | Reducing waiting time
5. Understanding the Kano Model
Before we designed the questionnaire, we made sure everyone in the group understood what each Kano category means, since we would use these same categories later to classify all of our survey responses. The Kano Model looks at how a feature's presence or absence changes user satisfaction. It is important to note that Kano only describes how users react, it does not by itself decide what should be built first; cost, risk, feasibility, and business priorities still matter and have to be considered alongside it.
Category | Meaning | Typical Reaction
Must-be (M) | Basic feature expected by users; its absence causes strong dissatisfaction. | Expected when present; users get frustrated when it is missing.
One-dimensional (O) | Satisfaction rises or falls directly with how well the feature performs. | Better performance means more satisfaction, and worse performance means clear dissatisfaction.
Attractive (A) | Not something users demand, but it delights them when it is there. | Happy when present; little to no dissatisfaction when it is missing.
Indifferent (I) | Has almost no effect on how satisfied a user feels. | Users barely notice whether it is present or absent.
Reverse (R) | Some users actually prefer that the feature does not exist. | Presence of the feature can reduce satisfaction for these users.
Questionable (Q) | The respondent's two answers contradict each other or are unclear. | The category cannot be determined reliably from that response.
6. Kano Questionnaire Design
For every feature we wrote two paired questions, a functional question that asks how the respondent would feel if the feature were present, and a dysfunctional question that asks how they would feel if it were absent. Both questions used the same five answer choices: I like it, I expect it / It must be that way, I am neutral, I can tolerate it / I can live with it, and I dislike it. We were careful to keep the wording plain and neutral so that we would not lead respondents toward a particular answer. The ten functional/dysfunctional pairs we actually used are shown below.
No. | Feature | Functional Question | Dysfunctional Question
1 | Course search | How would you feel if the system allowed you to search for courses by course code, title, or department? | How would you feel if the system did not allow you to search for courses by course code, title, or department?
2 | Remaining seats display | How would you feel if the system displayed the number of remaining seats for each course? | How would you feel if the system did not display the number of remaining seats for each course?
3 | Registration confirmation | How would you feel if the system provided confirmation after you successfully registered for a course? | How would you feel if the system did not provide confirmation after you registered for a course?
4 | SMS/email notification | How would you feel if the system sent SMS or email notifications about your course registration? | How would you feel if the system did not send SMS or email notifications about your course registration?
5 | Automatic course recommendations | How would you feel if the system provided automatic course recommendations based on your academic information? | How would you feel if the system did not provide automatic course recommendations?
6 | Dark mode | How would you feel if the course registration system provided a dark mode option? | How would you feel if the course registration system did not provide a dark mode option?
7 | Download timetable as PDF | How would you feel if the system allowed you to download your timetable as a PDF? | How would you feel if the system did not allow you to download your timetable as a PDF?
8 | Remember selected courses | How would you feel if the system remembered your selected courses before you submitted your final registration? | How would you feel if the system did not remember your selected courses before you submitted your final registration?
9 | Data preservation | How would you feel if the system preserved your registration data during a temporary network problem? | How would you feel if the system did not preserve your registration data during a temporary network problem?
10 | Fast peak-period response | How would you feel if the system responded quickly during busy registration periods when many students were using it? | How would you feel if the system did not respond quickly during busy registration periods?
7. Implementing the Questionnaire in Google Forms
We created a Google Form titled "Kano Analysis — University Course Registration System" with a short introduction explaining the purpose of the survey to respondents. For each of the ten features we added one functional and one dysfunctional question using the same five response options described above, and we kept respondent identification optional. Before sending the form out, two of us tested it ourselves to check the wording and confirm the response options worked correctly.
We shared the form with students and collected 40 complete and partial responses in total, more than the 15 to 30 the lab suggested as a minimum, which gave us a slightly larger sample to work with.
Google Form link: [Insert your Google Form link here]
8. Kano Evaluation Matrix
To turn a respondent's pair of answers into a single Kano category, we used the standard evaluation matrix below. The row is the answer to the functional question and the column is the answer to the dysfunctional question.
Functional \ Dysfunctional | Like | Expect | Neutral | Tolerate | Dislike
Like | Q | A | A | A | O
Expect | R | I | I | I | M
Neutral | R | I | I | I | M
Tolerate | R | I | I | I | M
Dislike | R | R | R | R | Q
For example, someone who says they would like the feature if present and dislike it if absent is classified as One-dimensional, since their satisfaction clearly rises and falls with the feature. Someone who says they would like it both present and absent is marked Questionable, because that pair of answers does not make logical sense on its own.
9. Analysing the Responses
We linked the form to a response spreadsheet and, following the lab instructions, kept the raw responses on their own sheet and built a separate sheet for the analysis instead of editing the raw data directly. We first classified a handful of response pairs by hand to make sure we understood the logic correctly, then applied the same matrix consistently to all 40 responses across all ten features. Our complete workbook (raw responses, the evaluation matrix, the full classification of every response, and the summary shown below) is attached alongside this report as a separate Excel file.
10. Kano Summary Results
After classifying every response we counted how many respondents fell into each Kano category, for each feature. A small number of respondents (between one and four out of forty, depending on the feature) skipped one of the two paired questions, so that particular response pair could not be classified and was left out of the count for that feature only.
Feature | A | O | M | I | R | Q | Dominant
Course search | 15 | 11 | 1 | 8 | 0 | 4 | Attractive (A)
Available-seat display | 12 | 9 | 4 | 9 | 0 | 4 | Attractive (A)
Registration confirmation | 5 | 12 | 5 | 10 | 2 | 4 | One-dimensional (O)
SMS/email notification | 9 | 9 | 2 | 13 | 1 | 4 | Indifferent (I)
Automatic recommendations | 8 | 8 | 1 | 12 | 3 | 4 | Indifferent (I)
Dark mode | 6 | 8 | 1 | 13 | 5 | 6 | Indifferent (I)
Download timetable | 8 | 11 | 5 | 7 | 1 | 6 | One-dimensional (O)
Remember selected courses | 9 | 8 | 3 | 10 | 3 | 4 | Indifferent (I)
Data preservation | 5 | 8 | 3 | 10 | 3 | 8 | Indifferent (I)
Fast peak-period response | 7 | 12 | 5 | 9 | 1 | 5 | One-dimensional (O)
11. Chart

Figure 1: Kano category distribution for all ten features (n = 40).
12. Interpretation of Major Findings
Course search and the remaining-seats display both came out Attractive, meaning students see these as a nice addition rather than something they absolutely demand, though in a system built specifically for registering for courses we would still treat both as central. Registration confirmation, downloading the timetable as a PDF, and fast response during peak registration periods all came out One-dimensional, which means the better these are built, the happier students will be, and the worse they are built, the more students will complain. This makes sense: confirmation, a working timetable download, and the system not slowing down during registration week are all things students directly experience and judge the system on.
SMS/email notifications, automatic course recommendations, dark mode, remembering selected courses, and preserving data during a network problem all came out Indifferent, meaning most students did not feel strongly either way about them. None of the ten features came out strongly as pure Must-be in our data, though registration confirmation and download timetable both had a fairly high Must-be count alongside their One-dimensional lean, which suggests some students already see these as basic expectations rather than bonus features.
13. Explaining One Questionable and One Indifferent Response Pattern
Questionable example: Data preservation during a temporary network problem had the highest number of Questionable responses of any feature in our survey (8 out of 40). We think this happened because the question describes a fairly specific and technical situation, a temporary network problem while registering, and some respondents may not have pictured the same scenario while answering the functional and dysfunctional versions of the question, leading to answers that contradicted each other. This does not mean the feature itself is a bad idea, it means we cannot rely on this particular set of responses to say confidently how students feel about it, and a clearer explanation in the question would likely reduce this number if we ran the survey again.
Indifferent example: Dark mode had the highest Indifferent count in our data (13 out of 40), tied with SMS/email notification. This fits what we expected going in, since dark mode is a display preference and has nothing to do with actually completing a registration. Students can register for their courses whether or not the interface has a dark theme, so most respondents said they would feel neutral or could tolerate it either way. It is worth noting dark mode also had a somewhat higher Reverse count than other features (5 out of 40), meaning a few students would actually prefer the system not to have it at all, possibly due to readability or accessibility concerns, which is a small but real signal worth keeping in mind.
14. Reflection: Using Kano Results for Requirements Prioritization
Working through this lab showed us that a Kano category by itself does not tell the whole story. Course search came out Attractive in our data, but we would not push it down the priority list, since it is one of the very first things a student does in this system and the whole point of the tool depends on it working well. On the other hand, registration confirmation and fast response during peak periods came out One-dimensional, and both also require real engineering effort, confirmation touches the registrar's approval process and fast response depends on the university's server infrastructure, so cost and technical feasibility matter here just as much as the Kano result. Features like dark mode, which came out clearly Indifferent, are reasonable to leave for later or drop entirely if the team is short on time, since building them would not move student satisfaction much either way. Overall, this lab made it clear that Kano results are one useful input into deciding what to build first, but they need to sit alongside cost, risk, dependencies, and business priorities rather than being used alone.

Software Requirements Engineering – Lab Report
Sources of Requirements + Kano Model — University Course Registration System
Group: Hudaibia, Sarah Arif, Eshaal Nazir, Abdul Samad
Submitted to: Sir Fahim Muhammad Khan : 24 Sept 2026
1. What we did
For this lab we had to find out where the requirements for a new university course registration system should come from, and then use the Kano Model to check how students actually feel about some possible features of it. We picked 8 sources, listed 10 candidate features, made a Kano questionnaire out of them, sent it out, and got 40 responses back. Below is everything we found.
2. Sources of requirements (8)
Source | Example | What we get from it
Students | The people who will actually use the system | What they need, what annoys them now
Registrar office | Registration staff | Rules, approvals, policies
Faculty | Course instructors | Prerequisites, seat limits
IT staff | University IT department | Security, servers, technical limits
Current system | The old manual process | What already works, what doesn't
Academic policies | University rules and deadlines | What the system must follow
Watching students register | Observing registration week | Real problems people run into
Survey | Our Kano questionnaire | What students actually want most
3. Candidate features (10)
These are the 10 features we picked, based on the sources above, and later put into our survey.
No. | Feature
1 | Search courses by code/title/department
2 | Show remaining seats
3 | Registration confirmation
4 | SMS/email notification
5 | Automatic course recommendations
6 | Dark mode
7 | Download timetable as PDF
8 | Remember selected courses
9 | Save data if network drops
10 | Fast response at peak times
4. The Kano questionnaire
For each of the 10 features above we made two questions, one asking how the student would feel if the feature WAS there, and one asking how they'd feel if it was NOT there. Both used the same 5 answers: I like it / I expect it / I am neutral / I can tolerate it / I dislike it. We built this in Google Forms, titled "Kano Analysis — University Course Registration System", tested it ourselves first, then sent it out to students.
Form link: [paste your Google Form link here]
5. How we classified answers
We used the standard Kano table below to turn each pair of answers into one letter (A/O/M/I/R/Q). This was done in a spreadsheet, not by hand, for all 40 responses.
Have it \ Don't have it | Like | Expect | Neutral | Tolerate | Dislike
Like | Q | A | A | A | O
Expect | R | I | I | I | M
Neutral | R | I | I | I | M
Tolerate | R | I | I | I | M
Dislike | R | R | R | R | Q
6. Results (n = 40)
A few people skipped a question or two here and there, so those specific answers were left out and not counted for that one feature.
Feature | A | O | M | I | R | Q | Dominant
Course search | 15 | 11 | 1 | 8 | 0 | 4 | Attractive
Seat display | 12 | 9 | 4 | 9 | 0 | 4 | Attractive
Registration confirmation | 5 | 12 | 5 | 10 | 2 | 4 | One-dimensional
SMS/email notification | 9 | 9 | 2 | 13 | 1 | 4 | Indifferent
Course recommendations | 8 | 8 | 1 | 12 | 3 | 4 | Indifferent
Dark mode | 6 | 8 | 1 | 13 | 5 | 6 | Indifferent
Download timetable | 8 | 11 | 5 | 7 | 1 | 6 | One-dimensional
Remember courses | 9 | 8 | 3 | 10 | 3 | 4 | Indifferent
Data preservation | 5 | 8 | 3 | 10 | 3 | 8 | Indifferent
Fast peak response | 7 | 12 | 5 | 9 | 1 | 5 | One-dimensional

7. What the results mean
Course search and the seat display came out as Attractive, students like having them but won't get too mad if they're basic, though for this system we'd still build both early since the whole app is built around them. Registration confirmation, downloading the timetable, and fast response at busy times all came out One-dimensional, so the better we do these, the happier students are, and the worse we do them, the more they complain. Everything else, notifications, recommendations, dark mode, remembering courses, saving data during network issues, came out mostly Indifferent, students don't care much either way.
Questionable example: "Save data if network drops" had the most Questionable answers (8 out of 40). We think it's because the question describes a specific situation and not everyone imagined the same thing when answering both parts, so their answers ended up contradicting each other.
Indifferent example: Dark mode had the most Indifferent answers (13 out of 40). Makes sense, it's just a look/theme thing and has nothing to do with actually registering for a class, so most people don't really care if it's there or not.
8. Does this decide what we build first?
Not on its own. Kano only tells us how students feel, it doesn't account for cost, time, or how hard something is to build. So even though course search is "just" Attractive, we'd still build it first since nothing else works without it. And something like dark mode being Indifferent means it's fine to leave for last, or skip it completely if we run out of time.

Sarah Arif | Questionnaire + Google Form
Eshaal Nazir | Spreadsheet + classification + chart
Abdul Samad | Write-up + reflection + final report

Software Requirement Engineering (Lab)





Submitted by: Abdul Samad 
Submitted to: Sir Fahim Muhammad Khan
Lab No. 5
Semester: V - BSSE (Group-A) 
Use Case Modeling
Session 2024 –2028 (Fall)


INSTITUTE OF MANAGEMENT SCIENCES 
HAYATABAD, PESHAWAR (2025)

Task 1 - Identify the System Boundary
System name: Smart Academic and Examination Management System (SAEMS).
Inside the boundary: The SAEMS use cases that support academic and examination activities, including course registration, course dropping, timetable and examination schedule viewing, instructor work, coordinator work, examination work, and administrator functions.
Outside the boundary: The actors that interact with SAEMS. The scenario specifically mentions the Identity Authentication Service and Bank Payment Gateway as external systems. The human actors are also outside the boundary.
Task 2 - Identify Actors

Actor | Type | Reason for Interaction
Student | Primary, human | Uses SAEMS for course search, registration, dropping courses, timetable and examination schedule.
Course Instructor | Primary, human | Uses SAEMS to view assigned courses and students, upload materials, submit attendance and enter marks.
Department Coordinator | Primary, human | Manages course offerings, instructor assignments and special registration/drop requests.
Examination Officer | Primary, human | Creates examination schedules, assigns rooms, publishes the timetable and records results.
System Administrator | Primary, human | Manages accounts, roles, permissions, configuration and system reports.
Identity AuthenticationService | Secondary, external system | Used when a user logs in and when password recovery is needed.
Bank Payment Gateway | Secondary, external system | Processes the student's outstanding dues payment and returns the payment result.



Task 3 - Identify Actor Goals / Candidate Use Cases

Actor | Candidate Goal / Use Case
Student | Search CoursesView Course DetailsRegister for CourseDrop CourseView TimetableView Examination Schedule
Course Instructor | View Assigned CoursesView Registered StudentsUpload Lecture MaterialsSubmit AttendanceEnter Internal Marks
Department Coordinator | Manage Course OfferingsAssign Instructors to CoursesReview Special RegistrationReview Special Drop Request
Examination Officer | Create Examination ScheduleAssign Examination RoomsPublish Examination TimetableRecord and Release Results
Actor | Candidate Goal / Use Case
System Administrator | Manage User AccountsManage Roles and PermissionsConfigure SystemGenerate System Reports
University User (all five human roles) | Log In

Task 4 - Draw the Basic Use Case Diagram
The supplied StarUML model is included below as the diagram used for this report.

Task 5 - Analyze «include» and «extend»
The relationships below follow the completed model. «include» is used for behavior that is required as part of the base use case. «extend» is used where the extra behavior happens only in a particular condition.

Extension | Base | Condition
Recover Password | Log In | Student forgot password
Join Waiting List | Register for Course | Course is full
Pay Outstanding Dues | Register for Course | Student has dues
Request Special Registration | Register for Course | Prerequisites missing
Submit Special Drop Request | Drop Course | Deadline has passed
Modify Examination Schedule | Publish Examination Timetable | Room or time conflict found
Base | Included
Register for Course | Check Registration Eligibility (prerequisites and seats)
Enter Internal Marks | Validate Marks Completeness
Publish Examination Timetable | Check Schedule Conflicts

These checks are kept as separate included use cases in the model. They could also be written as steps inside the fully dressed use case, but the important point is to keep the chosen approach consistent.
Task 6 - Consider Generalization
An abstract actor called University User is used for the five human roles. Student, Course Instructor, Department Coordinator, Examination Officer and System Administrator inherit the shared Log In use case from this general actor.
This also handles the case where one person performs more than one university role: the person can act through the relevant specialized actor roles.
Task 7 - Review the Model Like a Requirements Analyst
 System boundary is clearly defined.
 Actors are outside the system boundary.
 Use cases are inside the system boundary.
 Use case names describe meaningful goals.
 Each actor has a reason for interacting with SAEMS.
 User-interface actions are not used as separate use cases.
 «include» relationships are used for required checks.
 «extend» relationships are used for conditional or optional behavior.
 Relationship directions and labels are shown in the diagram.
 The diagram is kept as the supplied model rather than adding unrelated features.
Task 8 - Write One Use Case Description

Use Case Name | Register for Course
Primary Actor | Student
Goal | Register for a selected course successfully through SAEMS.
Preconditions | The student is logged in and has selected a course to register for.
Main Success Scenario | The student starts the course registration.SAEMS checks the student's identity, prerequisites and available seats.The registration is completed when the required checks are satisfied.SAEMS generates a registration confirmation.SAEMS updates the student's timetable.
Alternative / Exception Flows | If the course is full, the student may join the waiting list. If the student has outstanding dues, the dues are paid through the Bank Payment Gateway before registration is completed. If prerequisites are missing, the student may submit a special registration request.
Postconditions | The student is registered for the course and the timetable is updated.

Lab Reflection Questions
What is the difference between an actor and a user?
An actor is an external entity that interacts with the system to achieve a goal. A user is a person who uses the system. In a use case model, an actor can also be another system or an external service.
Why must actors normally be outside the system boundary?
The boundary shows what belongs to the system being modeled. Actors are outside because they interact with the system rather than being part of the system itself.
Why is “Register for Course” a stronger use case candidate than “Click Register Button”?
“Register for Course” describes a meaningful goal the student wants to complete. “Click Register Button” is only a user-interface action.
What is the practical difference between «include» and «extend»?
«include» is used when the included behavior is required as part of the base use case. «extend» is used when extra behavior happens only under a condition or is optional.
What mistake would occur if every system function were treated as a separate use case?
The model would contain too many small and unnecessary use cases. It would become harder to read and would mix internal system activities with meaningful user goals.
How does a Use Case Diagram differ from a fully dressed Use Case?
A use case diagram shows actors, use cases and their relationships at a high level. A fully dressed use case gives more detail about one use case, such as its actor, goal, preconditions, main steps, alternatives and postconditions.
7. What information does a Use Case Diagram intentionally leave out?
It leaves out the detailed step-by-step flow, alternative flows, preconditions and postconditions of each use case. Those details are written in the fully dressed use case.
Key Takeaway
Use case modeling focuses on who interacts with the system, what meaningful goals they want to achieve, and how those interactions are represented at a high level.

Smart University Academic & Examination Management System
A university is developing a Smart Academic and Examination Management System (SAEMS) that allows students to manage their academic activities through a single portal. A Student can log in to the system, search available courses, view course details, register for courses, drop registered courses, view their timetable, and check examination schedules. Before a student can register for a course, the system verifies the student's identity and checks whether the student has satisfied the required prerequisites and whether seats are available in the selected course. If a course is full, the student may request to be placed on a waiting list. If the student has outstanding university dues, the system asks the student to clear the dues before completing registration. The student can pay the dues through an external Bank Payment Gateway, which sends the payment result back to SAEMS. After successful registration, the system generates a registration confirmation and updates the student's timetable. A Course Instructor can log in, view the courses assigned to them, view the list of registered students, upload lecture materials, and submit attendance records. The instructor can also enter internal assessment marks, but before marks are submitted, the system validates that all required assessment components have been entered. If an instructor attempts to submit incomplete marks, the system displays an error and allows the instructor to correct them. A Department Coordinator manages course offerings, assigns instructors to courses, approves special course registrations, and reviews requests from students who want to register for courses despite missing prerequisites. The coordinator may approve or reject such requests. An Examination Officer creates examination schedules, assigns examination rooms, publishes the final examination timetable, and records examination results. Before publishing a timetable, the system checks for room and time conflicts. If a conflict is detected, the officer must modify the schedule before publication. A System Administrator manages user accounts, roles, permissions, and system configuration. The administrator can also generate system reports. The university's Identity Authentication Service is used whenever a user logs in, while the Bank Payment Gateway is used whenever a student makes an online payment. The system automatically sends email or SMS notifications to students and instructors after important events such as successful course registration, registration rejection, timetable publication, examination schedule changes, or release of examination results. In exceptional situations, such as a student forgetting their password, the student can initiate password recovery through the authentication service. Similarly, if a student attempts to drop a course after the university's deadline, the system does not normally allow the operation but provides an option to submit a special drop request to the Department Coordinator for approval. Different types of users have different permissions, and some users may perform more than one role within the university.
Student task
Ask your students to identify and model the system without being given the relationships explicitly. They should determine:
System boundary
Primary actors
Secondary actors
Human vs. external-system actors
Candidate use cases
Actor–use-case associations
<<include>> relationships
<<extend>> relationships
Actor generalization, if applicable
Appropriate use-case names
Any relationships that should not be modeled
At least one fully dressed use case from their diagram
Important challenge: Tell students that not every sentence in the scenario automatically becomes a use case. They must determine which behaviors represent meaningful user goals and which are merely internal system activities.

FILE 25/48: Lab Task 5.1\Lab Task 5 Scenario.docx

Smart University Academic & Examination Management System
A university is developing a Smart Academic and Examination Management System (SAEMS) that allows students to manage their academic activities through a single portal. A Student can log in to the system, search available courses, view course details, register for courses, drop registered courses, view their timetable, and check examination schedules. Before a student can register for a course, the system verifies the student's identity and checks whether the student has satisfied the required prerequisites and whether seats are available in the selected course. If a course is full, the student may request to be placed on a waiting list. If the student has outstanding university dues, the system asks the student to clear the dues before completing registration. The student can pay the dues through an external Bank Payment Gateway, which sends the payment result back to SAEMS. After successful registration, the system generates a registration confirmation and updates the student's timetable. A Course Instructor can log in, view the courses assigned to them, view the list of registered students, upload lecture materials, and submit attendance records. The instructor can also enter internal assessment marks, but before marks are submitted, the system validates that all required assessment components have been entered. If an instructor attempts to submit incomplete marks, the system displays an error and allows the instructor to correct them. A Department Coordinator manages course offerings, assigns instructors to courses, approves special course registrations, and reviews requests from students who want to register for courses despite missing prerequisites. The coordinator may approve or reject such requests. An Examination Officer creates examination schedules, assigns examination rooms, publishes the final examination timetable, and records examination results. Before publishing a timetable, the system checks for room and time conflicts. If a conflict is detected, the officer must modify the schedule before publication. A System Administrator manages user accounts, roles, permissions, and system configuration. The administrator can also generate system reports. The university's Identity Authentication Service is used whenever a user logs in, while the Bank Payment Gateway is used whenever a student makes an online payment. The system automatically sends email or SMS notifications to students and instructors after important events such as successful course registration, registration rejection, timetable publication, examination schedule changes, or release of examination results. In exceptional situations, such as a student forgetting their password, the student can initiate password recovery through the authentication service. Similarly, if a student attempts to drop a course after the university's deadline, the system does not normally allow the operation but provides an option to submit a special drop request to the Department Coordinator for approval. Different types of users have different permissions, and some users may perform more than one role within the university.
Student task
Ask your students to identify and model the system without being given the relationships explicitly. They should determine:
System boundary
Primary actors
Secondary actors
Human vs. external-system actors
Candidate use cases
Actor–use-case associations
<<include>> relationships
<<extend>> relationships  Actor generalization, if applicable
Appropriate use-case names
Any relationships that should not be modeled
At least one fully dressed use case from their diagram
Important challenge: Tell students that not every sentence in the scenario automatically becomes a use case. They must determine which behaviors represent meaningful user goals and which are merely internal system activities.

--- PAGE 1 ---
Smart University Academic & Examination Management System

A university is developing a Smart Academic and Examination Management System
(SAEMS) that allows students to manage their academic activities through a single
portal. A Student can log in to the system, search available courses, view course
details, register for courses, drop registered courses, view their timetable, and check
examination schedules. Before a student can register for a course, the system verifies
the student's identity and checks whether the student has satisfied the required
prerequisites and whether seats are available in the selected course. If a course is full,
the student may request to be placed on a waiting list. If the student has outstanding
university dues, the system asks the student to clear the dues before completing
registration. The student can pay the dues through an external Bank Payment Gateway,
which sends the payment result back to SAEMS. After successful registration, the
system generates a registration confirmation and updates the student's timetable. A
Course Instructor can log in, view the courses assigned to them, view the list of
registered students, upload lecture materials, and submit attendance records. The
instructor can also enter internal assessment marks, but before marks are submitted,
the system validates that all required assessment components have been entered. If an
instructor attempts to submit incomplete marks, the system displays an error and
allows the instructor to correct them. A Department Coordinator manages course
offerings, assigns instructors to courses, approves special course registrations, and
reviews requests from students who want to register for courses despite missing
prerequisites. The coordinator may approve or reject such requests. An Examination
Officer creates examination schedules, assigns examination rooms, publishes the final
examination timetable, and records examination results. Before publishing a timetable,
the system checks for room and time conflicts. If a conflict is detected, the officer
must modify the schedule before publication. A System Administrator manages user
accounts, roles, permissions, and system configuration. The administrator can also
generate system reports. The university's Identity Authentication Service is used
whenever a user logs in, while the Bank Payment Gateway is used whenever a student
makes an online payment. The system automatically sends email or SMS notifications
to students and instructors after important events such as successful course
registration, registration rejection, timetable publication, examination schedule
changes, or release of examination results. In exceptional situations, such as a student
forgetting their password, the student can initiate password recovery through the
authentication service. Similarly, if a student attempts to drop a course after the
university's deadline, the system does not normally allow the operation but provides
an option to submit a special drop request to the Department Coordinator for approval.
Different types of users have different permissions, and some users may perform
more than one role within the university.

Student task

Ask your students to identify and model the system without being given the
relationships explicitly. They should determine:

       System boundary
       Primary actors
       Secondary actors
      Human vs. external-system actors

USE CASE MODELING LAB
            LAB: USE CASE MODELING

                             Requirements Analysis and UML

Course                     Software Requirements /    Lab No.                05
                        SRE
Student Name                ________________________      Date                   Oct 6th-26
Section              A                        Duration                 90 minutes


1. Lab Overview
Use Case Modeling is a requirements-analysis technique used to describe how external actors interact with
a system to achieve meaningful goals. In this lab, you will analyze a real-world system scenario, identify
actors and their goals, establish relationships, and construct a UML Use Case Diagram.

2. Learning Objectives
   Identify actors that interact with a system.
   Distinguish actors from ordinary system components or internal processes.
   Identify meaningful user goals and convert them into candidate use cases.
   Define and draw the system boundary.
   Represent associations between actors and use cases.
  Understand when include, extend, and generalization relationships may be appropriate.
   Construct a clear UML Use Case Diagram using a modeling tool such as draw.io/Star UML etc.
  Review a use case model for completeness, consistency, and clarity.

3. Core Concepts to Understand Before the Lab
Concept                                      Meaning
Actor                                        An external entity that interacts with the system to
                                                        achieve a goal. An actor may be a person, another
                                                         system, or an external device/service.
Use Case                                   A meaningful goal or service that an actor wants to
                                                      accomplish through the system. Examples include
                                                           Register Course, Search Course, or View Timetable.
System Boundary                            A boundary that defines what belongs to the system
                                                     being modeled. Use cases are inside the boundary;
                                                             external actors are outside it.
Association                                 A relationship showing that an actor participates in or
                                                                interacts with a use case.
«include»                                        Used when a behavior is required as part of another use
                                                              case. Think: the included behavior must occur.
«extend»                                        Used when additional behavior occurs conditionally or
                                                             optionally in the context of a base use case.
Generalization                                         Represents a specialized actor or use case inheriting
                                                                characteristics or behavior from a more general one.

                                   Use Case Modeling Lab | Requirements Analysis and UML

--- PAGE 2 ---
USE CASE MODELING LAB
4. A Professional Modeling Mindset
Do not begin by asking: "What functions or buttons does the software have?"
Instead ask: "Who interacts with the system, and what meaningful goal are they trying to accomplish?"
For example, “Click Register Button” is normally a user-interface action rather than a meaningful use case.
“Register for Course” expresses a user goal and is therefore a stronger candidate use case.

5. Lab Scenario: University Course Registration System
   A university is developing an online Course Registration System. Students use the system to log in,
    search for available courses, view course information and available seats, register for courses, drop
    courses, and view their timetable. A Registrar manages course information and registration rules.
   Some courses may require a registration fee, which is handled through an external payment service.

6. Task 1 - Identify the System Boundary
Determine exactly what system is being modeled.
   Write the name of the system.
   State what is inside the system boundary.
   Identify entities that are outside the system boundary.
Deliverable: A labeled system boundary sketch.

7. Task 2 - Identify Actors
Read the scenario and identify all potential actors.
   List each actor.
   For every actor, explain why it is external to the system.
  Determine whether each actor is a human, external software system/service, or device.
Use the following table in your report:

Actor                          Type                           Reason for Interaction





                                   Use Case Modeling Lab | Requirements Analysis and UML

--- PAGE 3 ---
USE CASE MODELING LAB




8. Task 3 - Identify Actor Goals / Candidate Use Cases
For each actor, determine what meaningful goals they want to accomplish through the system.
Prepare an Actor–Goal table:

Actor                                             Candidate Goal / Use Case





9. Task 4 - Draw the Basic Use Case Diagram
Using Star UML, Eclipse Papyrus, Mermaid or another UML modeling tool, create the first version of your Use
Case Diagram.
  Draw the system boundary.
   Place actors outside the boundary.
   Place use cases inside the boundary.
  Connect actors to relevant use cases using associations.
  Use meaningful names for actors and use cases.
  Keep the diagram readable and avoid unnecessary crossing lines.

10. Task 5 - Analyze «include» and «extend»
Review your use cases and look for relationships between them.
For «include», ask: “Is this behavior required every time the base use case is performed?”
For «extend», ask: “Can the base use case complete without this additional behavior, with the extra
behavior occurring only under a condition?”
   Identify at least one possible «include» relationship if the scenario supports one.
   Identify at least one possible «extend» relationship if the scenario supports one.
    If you believe no relationship is justified, explain why rather than inventing one.
  Use correct UML direction and labels.


                                   Use Case Modeling Lab | Requirements Analysis and UML

--- PAGE 4 ---
USE CASE MODELING LAB
11. Task 6 - Consider Generalization
Examine the actors and use cases for possible generalization. Do not force a generalization relationship
merely to make the diagram more complex.
  Determine whether any actor is a specialized form of another actor.
    If applicable, draw the generalization relationship and justify it.
    If not applicable, state why generalization is unnecessary in this scenario.

12. Task 7 - Review Your Model Like a Requirements Analyst
Before submission, check your model against the following questions:
  ☐Is the system boundary clearly defined?
  ☐Are actors outside the system boundary?
  ☐Are use cases inside the system boundary?
  ☐Does every use case represent a meaningful goal?
  ☐Can you explain why every actor interacts with the system?
  ☐Have you confused user-interface actions with use cases?
  ☐Are «include» relationships truly mandatory/reusable behavior?
  ☐Are «extend» relationships truly conditional/optional behavior?
  ☐Are relationship directions and labels correct?
  ☐Is the diagram readable without excessive crossing lines?
  ☐Have you avoided unnecessary or duplicate use cases?

13. Task 8 - Write One Use Case Description
Select one important use case from your diagram and document it using the following structure.

Use Case Name
Primary Actor
Goal

                                                                ________________________________
Postconditions

14. Lab Reflection Questions
1.  What is the difference between an actor and a user?
2. Why must actors normally be outside the system boundary?
3. Why is “Register for Course” a stronger use case candidate than “Click Register Button”?
4.  What is the practical difference between «include» and «extend»?

USE CASE MODELING LAB
5.  What mistake would occur if every system function were treated as a separate use case?
6. How does a Use Case Diagram differ from a fully dressed Use Case?
7.  What information does a Use Case Diagram intentionally leave out?

19. Key Takeaway
   Use Case Modeling is about understanding WHO interacts with the system, WHAT
meaningful goals they want to achieve, and HOW those interactions are represented at a
                                   high level.

LAB 5
Requirements Elicitation Techniques
Requirement Engineering – Practical Lab
Item | Details
Course | Requirement Engineering
Lab | 05
Topic | Requirements Elicitation Techniques
Focus | Discovering requirements from evidence, users, existing systems, and prototypes

Instructor note: This lab is evidence-based. Students should understand that requirements elicitation is not guessing features; it is systematically discovering user and stakeholder needs.
Example:
Suppose a university wants to develop a Course Registration System. “We need a Course Registration System” is too general. A requirements engineer must discover what students, teachers, and administrators actually need.
What does a student do to register for a course?
What information does the student need before registering?
What does a teacher need to see?
What happens when a course is full?
What happens if registration fails?
What problems exist in the current process?
Different elicitation techniques provide different ways of finding these answers.
E.T in this Lab:
Category | Techniques | Simple question
Document-centric | System Archaeology; Perspective-based Reading; Reuse | What already exists, and what can we learn from it?
Observation | Field Observation; Apprenticing | What do users actually do in their real work?
Support | Mind Mapping; Workshop; CRC Cards; Audio/Video; Use Cases; Prototypes | How can we organize, discuss, model, or clarify requirements?

System Archaeology:
Simple definition: Study an existing or legacy system to discover what it already does and what requirements it supports.
What to do: Examine source code, documents, database structures, forms, reports, screenshots, workflows, or an existing application.
Example: An old Library Management System contains book search, issue, return, and fine calculation. These become candidate requirements for the new system.
Perspective Based Reading:
Simple definition: Read the same requirements document from a particular stakeholder perspective.
What to do: A developer looks for implementation clarity; a tester looks for testable information; a security specialist looks for authentication, authorization, privacy, and security gaps.
Example: “The system shall allow users to log in.” A tester asks what happens after an incorrect password; a security analyst asks about failed attempts and authentication controls.
Reuse:
Simple definition: Use previously developed requirements from a similar system when they are still relevant.
What to do: Reuse can reduce effort and cost, but every reused requirement must be checked for relevance and correctness.
Example: “Students shall view course materials” may be reused for a new LMS if it is still valid.
Field Observation:
Simple definition: Go to the user's real working environment and observe how the work is actually performed.
What to do: Record steps, information used, tools, problems, repeated work, delays, and workarounds. Observation can reveal hidden requirements.
Example: A librarian maintains a separate Excel sheet because the current system cannot produce a required report.
Apprenticing:
Simple definition: Learn by actually performing the stakeholder's work under their guidance.
What to do: The analyst behaves like an apprentice and questions unclear procedures while performing the task.
Example: The analyst performs patient registration and discovers that the same information must be entered repeatedly.
Mind Mapping:
Simple definition: Create a visual map of related requirements, terms, activities, and dependencies.
What to do: Start with a central system and branch into major areas and smaller requirements.
Example: Library System → Users, Books, Borrowing → Students, Librarian, Search, Issue, Return, Fine.
Workshop:
Simple definition: Bring stakeholders and requirements engineers together to discuss and agree on requirements.
What to do: Different stakeholder groups present needs, conflicts are discussed, and the group works toward agreement.
Example: Students request course search, teachers request enrollment lists, and administrators request seat management.
CRC Cards:
Simple definition: CRC means Class–Responsibility–Collaboration. Cards help identify possible classes and what each class is responsible for.
What to do: Class = object/concept; Responsibility = what it knows or does; Collaboration = other classes it works with.
Example: Student → register course, drop course, view timetable; collaborators: Course, Registration, Payment.
Audio/Video Recordings:
Simple definition: Record interviews or real work activities so they can be reviewed later.
What to do: Useful for fast processes or when details may be missed. Obtain permission and protect privacy/confidentiality.
Example: A permitted library recording reveals that staff check two systems before issuing a book.
Action Sequence/Use Case:
Simple definition: Describe how an actor interacts with the system to achieve a goal.
What to do: Identify actor, trigger, important actions/system responses, and expected outcome.
Example: Borrow Book → Student searches → system checks availability → student requests → system confirms borrowing.
Prototypes:
Simple definition: Create a rough version of an interface or workflow so stakeholders can react to something concrete.
What to do: Useful when stakeholders have a vague understanding of the proposed system. Feedback can reveal missing functions and information.
Example: A weather-app wireframe shows temperature and forecast; a user asks for hourly forecast and rain alerts.
Important Difference:
Technique | What the analyst does | Main question
System Archaeology | Studies an existing system | What does the existing system already do?
Field Observation | Watches users in their real environment | What do users actually do?
Apprenticing | Performs the work with guidance | What does the work feel like when I perform it?
Workshop | Discusses requirements with stakeholders | What can stakeholders agree on?
Prototype | Shows a rough proposed solution | What is missing or unclear when users see it?
Use Case | Models actor-system interaction | What interaction is needed to achieve a goal?

Task:
Each group applies one main elicitation technique and submits evidence plus candidate requirements.
System Archaeology: Library Management System:
A library is replacing an existing Library Management System. Examine available existing material and discover requirements that should be preserved or improved.
Student activity:
Examine an old system, screenshots, documents, forms, reports, sample database tables, or a provided mock system.
Identify at least 8 existing or candidate requirements.
Record the evidence supporting each requirement.
Identify at least 2 possible new/missing requirements based on observed limitations.
Do not simply copy a feature list; explain how the evidence led to each requirement.
Existing functionality / evidence | Candidate requirement | Evidence / source
Book search screen | System shall allow users to search books. | Existing search function
Issue form | System shall allow authorized staff to issue books. | Existing issue form
Fine report | System shall calculate/display overdue fines. | Existing report

Field Observation:
Observe how users perform a real or simulated process in an LMS or another university process such as library book issuing, course registration, assignment submission, or a student service.
Student activity:
Observe one complete process from start to finish.
Record who performs the task and what triggers it.
Record steps, information used, tools, repeated work, delays, errors, and workarounds.
Identify at least 5 problems or inefficiencies.
Convert at least 5 observations into potential requirements.
Observation questions:
Who performs the activity?
What starts the activity?
What information is required?
What tools or systems are used?
What steps are repeated?
Where does the user experience difficulty?
What happens when something goes wrong?
What manual workaround is used?


Prototype: Weather Forecasting Application
Create a low-fidelity prototype. The goal is not to build a working application; it is to use the prototype to discover and clarify requirements.
Student activity:
Create 4–5 simple screens using paper, PowerPoint, Balsamiq, Just in mind, Visio, Figma, Canva, or another suitable tool.
Include Home, Weather Details, Forecast, Alerts, and Settings/location.
Show the prototype to 2–3 potential users/classmates.
Ask what information or functions they expect.
Record feedback and convert it into at least 5 candidate requirements.
User feedback | Potential requirement
“I want hourly temperature.” | System shall display hourly weather information.
“I want rain alerts.” | System shall notify users about relevant rain/severe-weather alerts.
“I want to change the city.” | System shall allow users to select or change location.

Format:
1. System selected
2. Elicitation technique used
3. Stakeholders involved
4. Evidence collected
5. Observations/findings
6. Candidate requirements
7. Problems or limitations of the technique
8. Conclusion

Demo:
"Imagine that our university already has an old Course Registration System, but management wants us to develop a new and improved system. Before designing the new system, we need to understand what the existing system already provides."
Then explain:
"Instead of asking users immediately, we will first investigate the existing system. This investigation is called System Archaeology."
You can put this on your PowerPoint/board:
Existing Portal:
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│       UNIVERSITY REGISTRATION PORTAL        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                             │

"This is an existing system. Our job is to investigate it and discover what requirements it already supports."
Start Inspecting:
Go through each function.
Login:
You see:
Login
"What requirement can we derive from this?"
User should reach:
FR-01: The system shall allow students to log in using their credentials.
Explain:
Evidence: Login function exists in the existing system.
Candidate requirement: Student authentication is required.
Course Search:
You see:
Course Search
Ask:
"What does this tell us?"
Candidate requirement:
FR-02: The system shall allow students to search for available courses.
You can make it more detailed:
Students may search by course code, course title, department, or instructor.
But emphasize:
Don't invent these details unless we have evidence for them.
That's an important point in System Archaeology.
Course Selection:
Existing system has:
Course Selection
Candidate requirement:
FR-03: The system shall allow students to select a course for registration.
Ask:
"Why do we call this a candidate requirement?"
Because we have found evidence in the existing system, but we still need to validate whether this functionality should remain in the new system.
Add Course:
Existing function:
Add Course
Candidate requirement:
FR-04: The system shall allow students to add a selected course to their registration.
Then ask:
"What questions do we still have?"
User may say:
What if the course is full? 
What if the student has a prerequisite problem? 
What if the student selects the same course twice? 
Excellent:
"System archaeology gives us existing functionality, but it may not give us all the details. We may need other elicitation techniques to discover those details."
Drop Course:
Existing function:
Drop Course
Candidate requirement:
FR-05: The system shall allow students to drop a registered course.
"Do we know when students are allowed to drop a course?"
No.
Therefore:
This is where another elicitation technique may be needed.
For example, interview the registrar or observe the current process.
Timetable:
Existing function:
My Timetable
Candidate requirement:
FR-06: The system shall allow students to view their registered course timetable.
"What information might the timetable contain?"
User might suggest:
course name 
instructor 
day 
time 
room 
But now make an important teaching point:
"These are hypotheses. We should verify them rather than automatically treating every suggestion as a confirmed requirement."

Lab Task 6
University Course Registration System
This Level 1 DFD breaks the course registration system into four processes. It shows how student and course information is used to check a registration, save an accepted request, and prepare reports for the academic administration.
External entities
Student: Provides login credentials, requests the available courses, and submits selected course details. The student receives an authentication result, a course list, and a registration confirmation or a reason for rejection.
Academic Administration: Provides report criteria, such as a course or semester, and receives registration reports and course enrollment statistics.
Logical processes
1.0 Authenticate Student: Checks the supplied credentials against Student Records. It returns the authentication result and passes the authenticated student details to the next process.
2.0 Display Courses: Uses Course Records to prepare the available course list. It also passes the authenticated student details to the registration process so the selected courses can be linked to the correct student.
3.0 Validate and Record Registration: Checks the student’s academic record, course prerequisites, and available seats. If the request is valid, it saves the registration and updates seat availability. Otherwise, it returns the reason for rejection.
4.0 Generate Reports: Uses saved registration records and the administration’s report criteria to prepare registration reports and enrollment statistics.
Data stores
D1 Student Records: Stores student account information and academic history, including completed courses used for prerequisite checks.
D2 Course Records: Stores course information, prerequisites, and available seats. Seat availability is updated after a successful registration.
D3 Registration Records: Stores accepted registrations, including the student ID, course ID, and semester. These records are used to produce reports.
Level 1 Data Flow Diagram
Rectangles represent external entities, rounded rectangles represent processes, and open-ended parallel lines represent data stores.

Description of the data flows
Authentication: The student sends login credentials to Process 1.0. Student account data flows from D1 to this process for verification. The student receives an authentication result. Only authenticated student details are passed to Process 2.0.
Course viewing: The student sends a course list request to Process 2.0. Course details and seat availability are read from D2, and an available course list is returned to the student. The authenticated student details are then passed to Process 3.0.
Registration: The student sends selected course details to Process 3.0. This process reads the academic record from D1 and the prerequisites and available seats from D2. When the conditions are met, a new registration record flows to D3, updated seat availability flows to D2, and a confirmation is returned to the student.
Rejection: If a prerequisite is missing or no seat is available, Process 3.0 returns a rejection reason to the student. No registration record is created and the available seat count is not changed.
Reporting: The academic administration sends report criteria to Process 4.0. Registration records flow from D3 to this process. It returns the requested registration report and enrollment statistics.
Example of a registration
Suppose a student selects a course after logging in. The system checks whether the student has completed its prerequisite and whether a seat is available. If both checks pass, the registration is saved, the available seat count is reduced by one, and the student receives confirmation. If either check fails, the student receives a clear reason, such as “Prerequisite not completed” or “No seats available.”
DFD checks
Every arrow is labelled with the data being transferred, such as “Login credentials” or “Academic record.” Process names describe work performed by the system. External entities exchange data through processes rather than accessing a data store directly, and every process has both input and output data.
*-----------------------------------------------* 
The End

--- PAGE 1 ---
SRE Lab Task: Data Flow Diagram (DFD)


           Scenario: University Course Registration System

A university wants to develop an online Course Registration System through which
students can view available courses and register for their desired courses.

Students provide their login credentials to access the system. After successful
authentication, they can request a list of available courses and submit their selected
course details for registration.

The system retrieves student information from the Student Records database and
course information, including prerequisites and available seats, from the Course
Records database. Before accepting a registration request, the system verifies whether
the student has satisfied the course prerequisites and whether seats are available.

If all conditions are satisfied, the system records the registration in the Registration
Records database and sends a registration confirmation to the student. Otherwise, the
system rejects the request and provides an appropriate reason, such as unmet
prerequisites or no available seats.

The university's academic administration staff can request registration reports from
the system to review student registrations and course enrollment statistics.

                     Task: Level 1 DFD

  Decompose the main system into logical processes.
   Identify the required data stores.
  Connect processes, data stores, and external entities using appropriately labelled
    data-flow arrows.
  Ensure that every data flow represents data being transferred rather than an action
    or command.
